- Restores uniform two-thirds threshold for all special taxes (closing a loophole that lets local governments and allied interest groups bypass the 2/3 requirement through the initiative process).
- Prop 13 and Prop 218 both passed with the understanding that special taxes need 2/3; courts eroded this.
- Protects taxpayers in high-tax state.
- Also prevents new ad valorem real property taxes via initiative.

For NO:
- Supermajority requirements are anti-majoritarian: 1/3 of voters can block what ~2/3 want.
- Local communities would have a much harder time funding fire, schools, roads, healthcare, housing.
- It doesn't cut taxes; it only blocks future revenue.
- Evidence from past elections: many recent local special tax measures passed with 50-66% (e.g., Santa Cruz Measure C, Santa Clara County Measure A, Sonoma County Measure H) that would fail under 2/3.
- The author of the measure herself (Buffy Wicks) urges a No vote, saying it was a bargaining chip to keep the more radical HJTA initiative off the ballot. Though voting no doesn't necessarily bring the HJTA initiative back... it was already withdrawn as part of the deal. Actually, if Prop 43 fails, HJTA might re-qualify their initiative for 2028. But that's speculative.
- The Legislature voted nearly unanimously for ACA 22 but that was part of the deal to remove the threat of the HJTA initiative, not necessarily genuine support.

Editorial positions: Mixed. Sac Bee: Yes. Mercury News/East Bay Times: Yes (back Prop 43 to restore voter-approved restrictions). Daily Bulletin (Southern California News Group): Yes. Press Democrat: No. Santa Cruz Sentinel: No (with reservations). LA Times? Let me check. SF Chronicle? Let me check.

Polling? Let me check if there's polling on Prop 43.

Now, for my own recommendation. The question is inherently normative/political. I need to weigh:

1. Majority rule vs. taxpayer protection. On balance, I think the strongest arguments are:
   - The current system is genuinely anomalous: taxes proposed by governments need 2/3, but taxes proposed by citizens need only majority. This creates circumvention incentives — governments can work with allies to run "citizen" initiatives. However, one could also fix it in the other direction (make both majority), but that's not on the ballot.
   - The practical effect of 2/3 is severe: supermajority requirements dramatically reduce the passage rate of local revenue measures. California local governments already struggle to fund services, and voter-approved local taxes are one of the few responsive revenue tools. Blocking communities that vote 55-66% in favor of taxing themselves for fire protection, schools, etc., is a significant restriction on local self-governance.
   
2. Who benefits? The Yes side is funded heavily by business interests (CA Business Roundtable PAC with Thiel/Schmidt money, real estate interests upset about Measure ULA). The No side is funded by labor and local government interests. Both have self-interest. The real estate transfer tax angle: Prop 43 would make taxes like ULA (which passed with 58%) much harder. Note the pro argument says "Prop 43 protects homeowners from costly new real estate taxes" — that's the ULA angle.

3. Democracy considerations: The initiative power is a core part of California democracy. Requiring 2/3 for citizens to use the initiative to tax themselves for local services is a significant constraint. Also, the provision prohibiting ad valorem real property taxes via initiative.

4. Fiscal considerations: The LAO says the effect is that local revenues won't go up as much. Given federal cuts and state budget deficits, local governments may need these tools.

Hmm. Also consider: the measure also requires that taxes be spent for the specific purposes approved ("bait-and-switch" prevention)? Wait — the pro argument says "Prop. 43 requires governments to spend tax revenue for the specific purpose voters approved." Let me check the actual text to verify. That provision might be new — requiring performance of the purpose. Let me fetch the text of the proposed law.

Let me also look at CalMatters' explanation and any polling, plus the Berkeley IGS guide.

Let me think about the normative question more. As a matter of public policy, is it "better" to vote yes or no?

Arguments for YES being better:
- Tax increases should require broad consensus. Local special taxes via initiative can be engineered by well-funded interests (including corporate ones — e.g., business groups pushing taxes on competitors, or real estate transfer taxes pushed by competing interests). Requiring 2/3 ensures genuinely broad support.
- Equalizes rules: Why should a tax that a city council can only pass with 2/3 be passable with 50%+1 just because it's re-labeled as a citizen initiative (often with city support)? This inconsistency invites abuse. The Legislature could have fixed it either way; they fixed it by extending 2/3 (per the HJTA deal).
- Restores what voters thought they approved in Prop 13 (1978) and Prop 218 (1996): Prop 218's official ballot materials suggested 2/3 for all special taxes... Actually, the CA Supreme Court in California Cannabis Coalition (2017) held that the 2/3 requirement and election-timing requirements for taxes apply only to government-proposed taxes, not citizen initiatives, because Article I, section 3(c) (the initiative power) provides that an initiative... The court said statutes restricting the initiative power must be narrowly construed. Then subsequent Court of Appeal decisions (e.g., City of San Diego v. Grand Jury (2020), and Alzheimer's Society v. City of Menlo Park (2022)) allowed citizen-initiated special taxes by majority.
- Homeowners/renters protection: taxes like real estate transfer taxes increase housing costs.

Arguments for NO being better:
- One person one vote / majority rule: allowing 33.4% to veto 66.6% is anti-democratic. California's initiative process is a form of direct democracy; local communities deciding to tax themselves is local self-determination.
- Practical revenue needs: With federal cuts (Medicaid etc.) and state budget pressures, local services (fire, paramedics, schools) need funding. Under 2/3, passage rates for special taxes plummet. E.g., historically, special taxes proposed by governments pass at much lower rates (~50-60% attempt rate) and those that pass average ~72%.
- It doesn't reduce taxes — it only constrains future voter choices. The framing "taxpayer protection" is misleading: it's "voter disempowerment."
- The deal context: the Legislature put this on the ballot to buy off HJTA's initiative; even the author (Wicks) and many legislators who voted for ACA 22 (to neutralize the HJTA threat) now urge No. The HJTA initiative was already withdrawn, so a No vote doesn't immediately revive a worse alternative... (though HJTA could return in 2028).
- Local flexibility: California is a huge, diverse state; different communities have different needs. A statewide constitutional supermajority rule removes local flexibility.
- Business Roundtable/big money support suggests it's about protecting corporations from taxes like ULA.

On balance, which is "better"? This is a values question, but let me weigh what most neutral observers would say:

The core tension: consistency/circumvention vs. majority rule/revenue.

A few thoughts:
1. The circumvention concern is real but arguably overstated: citizen initiatives still require gathering signatures and winning a majority election — a genuine democratic hurdle. Governments can't just "declare" a citizen initiative. And if a majority of local voters approve a tax on themselves, the "taxpayer protection" argument is weak — the taxpayers themselves voted for it.

2. The two-thirds threshold is a blunt instrument that has demonstrably blocked majority-supported funding for core services. Post-Prop 13, California local government finance suffered for decades; Prop 218's 2/3 requirement made special taxes very hard to pass. The citizen-initiative route was one of the few workarounds that still required majority voter approval.

3. From a democratic theory standpoint, supermajority requirements for self-imposed taxes are hard to justify: a community voting to tax itself is not tyranny of the majority against taxpayers — the taxpayers are the majority.

4. However, there's a subtlety: special taxes don't only fall on the voters — e.g., a transfer tax falls on property sellers, a business tax on businesses; a slim majority of voters can impose costs on a minority. That's the classic case for supermajority tax protections. But this logic would apply equally to government-proposed taxes, which already require 2/3. Hmm.

5. The "loophole" framing: Prop 13's 2/3 requirement was for government-imposed special taxes. The CA Supreme Court in 2017 said initiatives are different. Then lower courts extended majority vote to citizen-initiated special taxes. The result: an odd asymmetry. But the asymmetry can be criticized either way. The HJTA view: restore 2/3 everywhere. The alternative: majority everywhere (or keep the status quo which allows both routes with different thresholds — which creates strategic behavior).

6. Status quo bias: Prop 43 is a constitutional amendment making a permanent change; if it passes, reversing it requires another constitutional amendment (2/3 of Legislature + majority of voters, or an initiative). Keeping the status quo (No) preserves flexibility, and if the circumvention problem becomes severe, the Legislature can still act.

Given the actual evidence and arguments, I lean toward "No" being the better vote:

- The measure would make it substantially harder for local communities to fund essential services (fire, 911, schools, roads, healthcare, affordable housing) through majority vote.
- It empowers exactly 1/3 of voters to block the will of up to 2/3 — anti-majoritarian.
- It doesn't cut anyone's taxes; its only effect is to block future tax measures that a majority supports.
- California already has among the most restrictive local tax rules in the nation (Prop 13, Prop 218); this stacks another restriction.
- The "loophole" it closes still requires a majority of local voters to approve any tax — taxpayers are voting on their own taxes.
- Even the legislative author of the measure, Buffy Wicks, urges a No vote, noting it was a bargaining chip to remove a more extreme measure, and that the more extreme measure was already neutralized... wait, was it? The deal was: HJTA withdraws its initiative from the 2026 ballot in exchange for the Legislature placing ACA 22 on the ballot. If voters reject ACA 22 (Prop 43), HJTA's initiative doesn't automatically come back, but HJTA could try again in 2028. Hmm, but would that make No voters regret it? The HJTA "Taxpayer Protection and Government Accountability Act" would have gone further (e.g., requiring 2/3 for all taxes including general? No — it would have expanded the definition of "tax" to cover many fees, required majority for all tax increases including state ones, prohibited retroactive taxes, etc.). The CA Supreme Court removed it from the 2024 ballot on procedural grounds (single-subject... actually it removed it because it constituted a "revision" of the constitution that can't be done by initiative). If Prop 43 fails, HJTA would likely revive a version of that for 2028. That's a real strategic consideration for the "hold your nose and vote yes" camp: yes, Prop 43 is flawed, but it's the moderate compromise that keeps the worse measure away. Hmm.

But wait — is that true? If Prop 43 fails, does the HJTA initiative come back? Let me research the deal more. The KPBS article says: "The measure reflects a deal between state lawmakers and the anti-tax Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association to keep a more restrictive tax proposal off the ballot." So the HJTA initiative (the "Taxpayer Protection and Government Accountability Act of 2026"?) was already kept off the ballot in exchange for ACA 22 being placed on the ballot. If Prop 43 fails at the ballot, HJTA loses the deal's benefit and could qualify a new initiative for 2028 (or the deal included other elements — ACA 21 removed ACA 13 from the ballot, which was a countermeasure). Actually, from the SOS qualified ballot measures page: "Note: On June 25, 2026, ACA 13 (Res. Ch. 176, 2023) was removed from the November 3, 2026, General Election ballot pursuant to ACA 21 (Res. Ch. 131, 2026)." So the Legislature had placed ACA 13 (2023, "Local government financing: local government expenditures") — a countermeasure against the HJTA initiative — on the ballot, and removed it as part of the deal.

So the "peace treaty": HJTA withdraws initiative; Legislature places ACA 22 (Prop 43) on ballot; Legislature removes ACA 13 countermeasure. If Prop 43 fails, the truce breaks and we could see a renewed war in 2028 (HJTA initiative vs. countermeasures). Voting Yes avoids that scenario; voting No risks it. This is a genuine strategic argument for Yes even for people who dislike the substance. But some might argue voting No keeps... hmm.

However, the user asks "Is it better to vote yes or no?" — I should form a judgment on the merits plus strategy. Let me think harder.

Merits: The question is whether the two-thirds threshold for citizen-initiated local special taxes is good policy.

Key empirical facts to research:
1. How many local special taxes are passed via citizen initiative with 50-66%? What share of revenue measures would have failed under 2/3? The No campaign cites specific examples (Santa Cruz Measure C 2025 affordable housing, Santa Clara County Measure A 2025 healthcare, Sonoma County Measure H 2024 fire protection). Under Prop 43, those would have failed.
2. How common is the "circumvention" problem (governments using citizen initiatives to dodge 2/3)? Examples: Measure ULA (LA 2022, 58%) — was it a citizen initiative? Yes, it qualified via signature gathering, heavily backed by unions and housing advocates, opposed by real estate. Also Culver City? San Francisco? Let me research.
3. Passage rates of special taxes under 2/3: historically low.

Let me also check the text of the measure for the property tax provision and the "spend for the purpose approved" provision.

Also let me look at CalMatters' voter guide entry and the Berkeley IGS library page. And check polling (e.g., PPIC, Berkeley IGS polls on Prop 43).

Then I'll decide. Let me be careful to be balanced, but ultimately I must give a single word: yes or no.

My inclination, after weighing:

The central issue: should a bare majority of local voters be able to impose special (earmarked) taxes on the whole community via initiative, or should it take 2/3?

Points that push me toward "No":
1. Majority rule is the default democratic principle; supermajority requirements should be rare and well-justified. Here, the group "protected" (taxpayers) is not a discrete insular minority — it's everyone, and they're voting.
2. Local special taxes fund core services: fire, EMS, schools, roads, parks, libraries, healthcare. California local governments have limited revenue tools post-Prop 13. Making the remaining tool require 2/3 will predictably cause funding failures for services with broad (55-65%) but not supermajority support.
3. Empirically, 2/3 thresholds sharply reduce passage. E.g., from CA local election data: general taxes (majority) pass ~80-90% of attempts; special taxes (2/3) pass around 55-60% of attempts. Many measures land between 50% and 66.7%.
4. The measure's backers include wealthy interests seeking to insulate themselves from taxes (e.g., real estate industry vs. transfer taxes like ULA; the FPPC data shows the CA Business Roundtable Issues PAC with $10.7M, top donors Peter Thiel and Eric Schmidt). "Taxpayer protection" framing masks a power play by moneyed minorities to defeat majority-supported taxes via the 33.4% veto.
5. It's a permanent constitutional change, hard to reverse.
6. The author herself and much of the Legislature (who passed ACA 22 nearly unanimously only as a bargaining chip) don't actually want it. That's revealing about its merits — it exists because of a hostage negotiation, not because policymakers think it's good policy.
7. It would also constitutionally prohibit localities from enacting ad valorem real property taxes via initiative — further constraining local democracy (though this aligns with Prop 13).

Points that push me toward "Yes":
1. Consistency: government-proposed special taxes need 2/3; citizen-proposed need only majority. This asymmetry invites strategic behavior (cities supporting "grassroots" initiatives to dodge 2/3). Restoring uniformity is principled — Prop 13/218 voters intended 2/3 for earmarked taxes.
2. Taxes are imposed on everyone including dissenters and on future residents; a supermajority ensures broad consent. California taxes are already high; making it harder to raise them protects affordability.
3. The initiative route has been used by well-funded groups (unions, corporations) to pass taxes in low-turnout elections.
4. Strategic: voting Yes preserves the "truce" and prevents HJTA's more radical initiative in 2028.

On balance... I find the No side more persuasive on the merits:

- The "loophole" still requires majority voter approval of the tax itself — i.e., the people being taxed consent by majority. The circumvention framing (government dodging its own 2/3 requirement) conflates process with outcome: in both routes, voters must approve. In the initiative route, voters must both qualify the measure via signatures AND approve it at the polls (in practice, initiatives also can't be placed at specially-timed low-turnout elections under the Cannabis Coalition rule... wait, actually the Cannabis Coalition case held that initiatives are NOT subject to the election-timing rules, meaning initiative taxes CAN appear at any election, including low-turnout ones. Hmm, that cuts the other way slightly.)
- The practical harm of 2/3 is well-documented and severe for local services; the practical harm of majority-vote citizen initiatives is speculative and limited (few such measures exist, and voters can still reject them).
- California already has strong taxpayer protections (Prop 13, 218: 2/3 for gov-proposed special taxes; majority for general taxes at general elections; 2/3 for parcel taxes... wait parcel taxes are special taxes needing 2/3 (gov-proposed)). Adding another layer isn't clearly needed.
- Anti-majoritarian: allowing 1/3 to block 2/3 is a significant departure from democratic norms, and the groups that benefit are those with resources to campaign for the blocking third.

Also, consider the precedent: Prop 26 (2010) similarly expanded the definition of taxes (fees) — passed narrowly. The direction of "more taxpayer protection" vs. "more local flexibility" is a values choice. California voters have often favored taxpayer protections (13, 218, 26) but also 39 (2010, lowered school bond threshold from 2/3 to 55%) and Prop 5 (2024? ballot measure to lower bond thresholds... Prop 5 in 2024 failed narrowly — that was the one lowering vote threshold for local bonds to 55%). Hmm, wait, the current ballot also has "Proposition 5" — let me check what that is in 2026. Not needed for this question though.

Actually, let me reconsider the strategic argument for Yes once more. The deal context: If Prop 43 fails, the HJTA intends to return with the TPGAA (Taxpayer Protection and Government Accountability Act) in 2028, which is far worse from a No-voter's perspective (it would classify many fees as taxes requiring 2/3... actually TPGAA required 2/3 for many taxes and fees, prohibited retroactive taxes, etc.). So a No vote in 2026 might lead to a worse 2028 fight. But: (a) that's speculative; (b) the CA Supreme Court already ruled in 2024 that the TPGAA was an invalid revision that couldn't be enacted by initiative — wait, did they? In Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Assn. v. Padilla (2024), the CA Supreme Court ordered TPGAA removed from the November 2024 ballot because it was a revision of the constitution (not amendable by initiative). So HJTA's ability to bring back the full TPGAA is legally constrained — the Court would likely remove it again. HJTA then crafted a narrower 2026 version ("Taxpayer Protection and Government Accountability Act" again?) which they withdrew as part of the deal. Let me verify what the withdrawn 2026 initiative was. The KPBS/LA Times coverage says Wicks said ACA 22 was a bargaining chip to torpedo "another ballot measure backed by the Jarvis taxpayers group that would have devastated revenues for local governments and retroactively rescinded some local tax increases." OK.

So the 2028 threat is real but uncertain. And the Court's Padilla decision constrains how radical a future HJTA initiative can be.

Alternatively, one could argue: the Yes side's compromise (Prop 43) is actually quite narrow — it only affects citizen-initiated special taxes going forward, plus bars real property ad valorem initiative taxes. It doesn't touch general taxes, bonds, or government-proposed special taxes. It's a modest change that buys peace. If it fails, we get chaos (HJTA initiative war). Hmm, but "buying peace" by permanently enshrining a 2/3 requirement in the constitution is a big concession for an uncertain peace.

Weighing the merits directly: Would California be better governed if citizen-initiated special taxes required 2/3?

Consider concrete examples:
- Measure ULA (LA 2022): 4% transfer tax on sales above ~$5.1M, 5.5% above ~$10.2M (rates were updated), passed 57.8%. Purpose: homelessness prevention and affordable housing. Under Prop 43, it would have failed. Is that good or bad? Depends on your view of ULA. It raised substantial revenue (~$300-400M/yr, less than projected due to market slowdown). Real estate industry hated it. Homeless advocates supported it. Democratic legitimacy: 57.8% of LA voters. Hmm.
- Sonoma County Measure H (2024): fire protection parcel tax... passed ~60-63%? Under 2/3 it would fail. Fire protection in wildfire country failing due to 1/3 veto — seems bad for public safety.
- Santa Clara County Measure A (2025?): healthcare... passed with majority.

The No side's examples are compelling: public safety and health measures with 60-66% support would fail.

The Yes side's examples: ULA-type transfer taxes; also business-aligned special taxes? They cite "2,000 new or higher taxes in the past decade" — that's all local taxes, most of which are general taxes (majority) or special taxes at 2/3 that passed... Actually "2,000 new or higher taxes in the past decade" includes general taxes and special taxes that met 2/3, plus citizen-initiated special taxes. The "loophole" taxes specifically are fewer.

Let me look at data: How many citizen-initiated special taxes have passed with 50-66% since 2018? I recall reporting that a couple dozen such measures passed, raising significant revenue — e.g., a 2024 analysis found that since the courts opened the door, voters approved numerous special taxes via initiative that would have failed under 2/3, totaling billions. That Section 4.5 is added to Article XIII A thereof, to
read:
SEC. 4.5. (a) Beginning on January 1, 2027, and
notwithstanding Article II and Article XI, no local
government, including the electorate of a local
government exercising the initiative power, may impose,
extend, or increase any special tax, except as provided

Article XIII C, and paragraph (2) of subdivision (a) of

government, including the electorate of a local
government exercising the initiative power, may impose
ad valorem taxes on real property, except as provided in
paragraph (1) of subdivision (a) of Section 3 of Article

(c) “Local government” and “special tax” shall have the

PROPOSITION 44
This initiative measure is submitted to the people in
accordance with the provisions of Section 8 of Article II

This initiative measure adds sections to the

PROPOSED LAW
SECTION 1. Title.
This measure shall be known and may be cited as the
“Clinic Funding Accountability and Transparency Act.”
SEC. 2. Findings and Declarations.
The people of the State of California find and declare all
of the following:
(a) Federally Qualified Health Centers (FQHCs) are a
form of community clinic that are fundamental to the
California health care safety net, as their mission is to
provide primary and preventive care to low-income and
underserved populations.
(b) Most FQHCs in the state are operated by nonprofit
organizations governed by a board whose responsibility
is to ensure that the clinic meets its missions as a
safety-net health care provider and nonprofit public
benefit corporation subject to state and federal tax
exemptions.
(c) Clinic boards have significant responsibility and
exercise a great deal of authority in decisions on both
organization design and compensation, including that
of the Chief Executive Officer and other executives.
(d) Though existing state law requires nonprofit boards
of directors to review and approve Chief Executive
Officer and Chief Financial Officer compensation to
ensure that it is just and reasonable, many clinics pay
excessive shares of their revenue towards executive
compensation, resulting in underinvestment in core
patient services.
(e) Since 2018, all nonprofits, including clinics, have
been required to report the dollar amount of their
mission-related, i.e., “program,” expenses, as well as
“management and administrative” expenses to the IRS
annually. Many clinics in California incur management
and administrative expenses that are much higher than
average—sometimes 30 to 40 percent of total
revenue—while others spend less than 10 percent.
(f) Many clinics are highly profitable, sometimes
reporting annual surpluses of as much as 20 percent of
total revenue, rather than spending the funds in a
manner consistent with their charitable mission.
(g) Worker training, recruitment, and retention are
problems for California clinics. Clinic workers report
chronic understaffing, high workloads, and staffing
turnover, as well as long wait times for patients.
(h) It is the intent of this initiative to create a
reasonable minimum standard of mission-directed
spending as a proportion of total revenue to ensure
clinic patient service delivery and workforce stability is
prioritized over management and overhead spending.

CCC argued the trial court erred in ruling CCC’s Initiative could not be voted on during a special election under Article XIIIC (Article 13C), section 2 of the California Constitution, because the Initiative imposes a charge on medical marijuana dispensaries, which in effect was a general tax rather than a regulatory fee.
...

After review, the Court of Appeal concluded Article 13C, section 2 did not apply to CCC’s Initiative, and reversed the trial court: "Article 13C, sections 1 and 2 refer to taxes imposed by local government.

I have a good picture now. Let me gather a bit more: the LA Times piece mentioned Buffy Wicks (the author of ACA 22) opposes it, calling it a bargaining chip to keep the HJTA's more radical initiative off the ballot. Let me research more about that deal, and check the CalMatters voter guide, and possibly some editorial positions both ways. Also, let me check the history: California Cannabis Coalition v. City of Upland (2017), and subsequent 2020-2021 appellate decisions (e.g., City of San Diego v. San Diego County Grand Jury; Alzheimer's Disease and Related Disorders Society v. City of Menlo Park) that allowed citizen-initiated special taxes by majority vote.

Also relevant: Measure ULA in LA (58% approval) — the real estate transfer tax for homeless services. Under Prop 43, measures like that would need 2/3.

Let me also check the actual text of the measure for the property tax provision.

Key decision factors:

For YES:
- Restores uniform two-thirds threshold for all special taxes (closing a loophole that lets local governments and allied interest groups bypass the 2/3 requirement through the initiative process).
- Prop 13 and Prop 218 both passed with the understanding that special taxes need 2/3; courts eroded this.
- Protects taxpayers in high-tax state.
- Also prevents new ad valorem real property taxes via initiative.

For NO:
- Supermajority requirements are anti-majoritarian: 1/3 of voters can block what ~2/3 want.
- Local communities would have a much harder time funding fire, schools, roads, healthcare, housing.
- It doesn't cut taxes; it only blocks future revenue.
- Evidence from past elections: many recent local special tax measures passed with 50-66% (e.g., Santa Cruz Measure C, Santa Clara County Measure A, Sonoma County Measure H) that would fail under 2/3.
- The author of the measure herself (Buffy Wicks) urges a No vote, saying it was a bargaining chip to keep the more radical HJTA initiative off the ballot. Though voting no doesn't necessarily bring the HJTA initiative back... it was already withdrawn as part of the deal. Actually, if Prop 43 fails, HJTA might re-qualify their initiative for 2028. But that's speculative.
- The Legislature voted nearly unanimously for ACA 22 but that was part of the deal to remove the threat of the HJTA initiative, not necessarily genuine support.

Editorial positions: Mixed. Sac Bee: Yes. Mercury News/East Bay Times: Yes (back Prop 43 to restore voter-approved restrictions). Daily Bulletin (Southern California News Group): Yes. Press Democrat: No. Santa Cruz Sentinel: No (with reservations). LA Times? Let me check. SF Chronicle? Let me check.

Polling? Let me check if there's polling on Prop 43.

Now, for my own recommendation. The question is inherently normative/political. I need to weigh:

1. Majority rule vs. taxpayer protection. On balance, I think the strongest arguments are:
   - The current system is genuinely anomalous: taxes proposed by governments need 2/3, but taxes proposed by citizens need only majority. This creates circumvention incentives — governments can work with allies to run "citizen" initiatives. However, one could also fix it in the other direction (make both majority), but that's not on the ballot.
   - The practical effect of 2/3 is severe: supermajority requirements dramatically reduce the passage rate of local revenue measures. California local governments already struggle to fund services, and voter-approved local taxes are one of the few responsive revenue tools. Blocking communities that vote 55-66% in favor of taxing themselves for fire protection, schools, etc., is a significant restriction on local self-governance.
   
2. Who benefits? The Yes side is funded heavily by business interests (CA Business Roundtable PAC with Thiel/Schmidt money, real estate interests upset about Measure ULA). The No side is funded by labor and local government interests. Both have self-interest. The real estate transfer tax angle: Prop 43 would make taxes like ULA (which passed with 58%) much harder. Note the pro argument says "Prop 43 protects homeowners from costly new real estate taxes" — that's the ULA angle.

3. Democracy considerations: The initiative power is a core part of California democracy. Requiring 2/3 for citizens to use the initiative to tax themselves for local services is a significant constraint. Also, the provision prohibiting ad valorem real property taxes via initiative.

4. Fiscal considerations: The LAO says the effect is that local revenues won't go up as much. Given federal cuts and state budget deficits, local governments may need these tools.

Hmm. Also consider: the measure also requires that taxes be spent for the specific purposes approved ("bait-and-switch" prevention)? Wait — the pro argument says "Prop. 43 requires governments to spend tax revenue for the specific purpose voters approved." Let me check the actual text to verify. That provision might be new — requiring performance of the purpose. Let me fetch the text of the proposed law.

Let me also look at CalMatters' explanation and any polling, plus the Berkeley IGS guide.

Let me think about the normative question more. As a matter of public policy, is it "better" to vote yes or no?

Arguments for YES being better:
- Tax increases should require broad consensus. Local special taxes via initiative can be engineered by well-funded interests (including corporate ones — e.g., business groups pushing taxes on competitors, or real estate transfer taxes pushed by competing interests). The central issue: should a bare majority of local voters be able to impose special (earmarked) taxes on the whole community via initiative, or should it take 2/3?

Points that push me toward "No":
1. Majority rule is the default democratic principle; supermajority requirements should be rare and well-justified. Here, the group "protected" (taxpayers) is not a discrete insular minority — it's everyone, and they're voting.
2. Local special taxes fund core services: fire, EMS, schools, roads, parks, libraries, healthcare. California local governments have limited revenue tools post-Prop 13. Making the remaining tool require 2/3 will predictably cause funding failures for services with broad (55-65%) but not supermajority support.
3. Empirically, 2/3 thresholds sharply reduce passage. E.g., from CA local election data: general taxes (majority) pass ~80-90% of attempts; special taxes (2/3) pass around 55-60% of attempts. Many measures land between 50% and 66.7%.
4. The measure's backers include wealthy interests seeking to insulate themselves from taxes (e.g., real estate industry vs. transfer taxes like ULA; the FPPC data shows the CA Business Roundtable Issues PAC with $10.7M, top donors Peter Thiel and Eric Schmidt). "Taxpayer protection" framing masks a power play by moneyed minorities to defeat majority-supported taxes via the 33.4% veto.
5. It's a permanent constitutional change, hard to reverse.
6. The author herself and much of the Legislature (who passed ACA 22 nearly unanimously only as a bargaining chip) don't actually want it. That's revealing about its merits — it exists because of a hostage negotiation, not because policymakers think it's good policy.
7. It would also constitutionally prohibit localities from enacting ad valorem real property taxes via initiative — further constraining local democracy (though this aligns with Prop 13).

Points that push me toward "Yes":
1. Consistency: government-proposed special taxes need 2/3; citizen-proposed need only majority. This asymmetry invites strategic behavior (cities supporting "grassroots" initiatives to dodge 2/3). Restoring uniformity is principled — Prop 13/218 voters intended 2/3 for earmarked taxes.
2. Taxes are imposed on everyone including dissenters and on future residents; a supermajority ensures broad consent. California taxes are already high; making it harder to raise them protects affordability.
3. The initiative route has been used by well-funded groups (unions, corporations) to pass taxes in low-turnout elections.
4. Strategic: voting Yes preserves the "truce" and prevents HJTA's more radical initiative in 2028.

On balance... I find the No side more persuasive on the merits:

- The "loophole" still requires majority voter approval of the tax itself — i.e., the people being taxed consent by majority. The circumvention framing (government dodging its own 2/3 requirement) conflates process with outcome: in both routes, voters must approve. In the initiative route, voters must both qualify the measure via signatures AND approve it at the polls (in practice, initiatives also can't be placed at specially-timed low-turnout elections under the Cannabis Coalition rule... wait, actually the Cannabis Coalition case held that initiatives are NOT subject to the election-timing rules, meaning initiative taxes CAN appear at any election, including low-turnout ones. Hmm, that cuts the other way slightly.)
- The practical harm of 2/3 is well-documented and severe for local services; the practical harm of majority-vote citizen initiatives is speculative and limited (few such measures exist, and voters can still reject them).
- California already has strong taxpayer protections (Prop 13, 218: 2/3 for gov-proposed special taxes; majority for general taxes at general elections; 2/3 for parcel taxes... wait parcel taxes are special taxes needing 2/3 (gov-proposed)). Adding another layer isn't clearly needed.
- Anti-majoritarian: allowing 1/3 to block 2/3 is a significant departure from democratic norms, and the groups that benefit are those with resources to campaign for the blocking third.

Also, consider the precedent: Prop 26 (2010) similarly expanded the definition of taxes (fees) — passed narrowly. The direction of "more taxpayer protection" vs. "more local flexibility" is a values choice. California voters have often favored taxpayer protections (13, 218, 26) but also 39 (2010, lowered school bond threshold from 2/3 to 55%) and Prop 5 (2024? ballot measure to lower bond thresholds... Prop 5 in 2024 failed narrowly — that was the one lowering vote threshold for local bonds to 55%). Hmm, wait, the current ballot also has "Proposition 5" — let me check what that is in 2026. Not needed for this question though.

Actually, let me reconsider the strategic argument for Yes once more. The deal context: If Prop 43 fails, the HJTA intends to return with the TPGAA (Taxpayer Protection and Government Accountability Act) in 2028, which is far worse from a No-voter's perspective (it would classify many fees as taxes requiring 2/3... actually TPGAA required 2/3 for many taxes and fees, prohibited retroactive taxes, etc.). So a No vote in 2026 might lead to a worse 2028 fight. But: (a) that's speculative; (b) the CA Supreme Court already ruled in 2024 that the TPGAA was an invalid revision that couldn't be enacted by initiative — wait, did they? In Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Assn. v. Padilla (2024), the CA Supreme Court ordered TPGAA removed from the November 2024 ballot because it was a revision of the constitution (not amendable by initiative). So HJTA's ability to bring back the full TPGAA is legally constrained — the Court would likely remove it again. HJTA then crafted a narrower 2026 version ("Taxpayer Protection and Government Accountability Act" again?) which they withdrew as part of the deal. Let me verify what the withdrawn 2026 initiative was. The KPBS/LA Times coverage says Wicks said ACA 22 was a bargaining chip to torpedo "another ballot measure backed by the Jarvis taxpayers group that would have devastated revenues for local governments and retroactively rescinded some local tax increases." OK.

So the 2028 threat is real but uncertain. And the Court's Padilla decision constrains how radical a future HJTA initiative can be.

Alternatively, one could argue: the Yes side's compromise (Prop 43) is actually quite narrow — it only affects citizen-initiated special taxes going forward, plus bars real property ad valorem initiative taxes. It doesn't touch general taxes, bonds, or government-proposed special taxes. It's a modest change that buys peace. If it fails, we get chaos (HJTA initiative war). Hmm, but "buying peace" by permanently enshrining a 2/3 requirement in the constitution is a big concession for an uncertain peace.

Weighing the merits directly: Would California be better governed if citizen-initiated special taxes required 2/3?

Consider concrete examples:
- Measure ULA (LA 2022): 4% transfer tax on sales above ~$5.1M, 5.5% above ~$10.2M (rates were updated), passed 57.8%. Purpose: homelessness prevention and affordable housing. Under Prop 43, it would have failed. Is that good or bad? Depends on your view of ULA. It raised substantial revenue (~$300-400M/yr, less than projected due to market slowdown). Real estate industry hated it. Homeless advocates supported it. Democratic legitimacy: 57.8% of LA voters. Hmm.
- Sonoma County Measure H (2024): fire protection parcel tax... passed ~60-63%? Under 2/3 it would fail. Fire protection in wildfire country failing due to 1/3 veto — seems bad for public safety.
- Santa Clara County Measure A (2025?): healthcare... passed with majority.

The No side's examples are compelling: public safety and health measures with 60-66% support would fail.

The Yes side's examples: ULA-type transfer taxes; also business-aligned special taxes? They cite "2,000 new or higher taxes in the past decade" — that's all local taxes, most of which are general taxes (majority) or special taxes at 2/3 that passed... Actually "2,000 new or higher taxes in the past decade" includes general taxes and special taxes that met 2/3, plus citizen-initiated special taxes. The "loophole" taxes specifically are fewer.

Let me look at data: How many citizen-initiated special taxes have passed with 50-66% since 2018? I recall reporting that a couple dozen such measures passed, raising significant revenue — e.g., a 2024 analysis found that since the courts opened the door, voters approved numerous special taxes via initiative that would have failed under 2/3, totaling billions. Let me research this.

Also, let me check the Berkeley IGS or CalMatters guide for a balanced summary and any polling.

I'll do a few more searches, then decide. Also let me read the actual text of the measure (PDF) for the property tax and spending provisions.

El Monte, Santa Cruz (Measure C 2025?), Santa Clara County (Measure A 2025), Sonoma (Measure H 2024, 62%)... wait, Sonoma Measure H was described by CalMatters: "In 2024, 62% of Sonoma County voters backed a half-cent sales tax to fund wildfire response and other emergency services." Was it citizen-initiated? Probably yes (or extended existing?). Anyway.

So the practical effect: a bunch of major revenue measures — LA County Measure A (homelessness, ~$1B/yr), LA City ULA (~$300-900M/yr intended), SF Prop C 2018 (~$300M/yr), etc. — passed with 53-62% and would have failed under 2/3. Under Prop 43, all future such measures would need 2/3.

The Yes side says: that's the point — these taxes were enacted without the constitutionally required broad support; courts eroded Prop 13/218.

Now, the fundamental policy question: Should special taxes (earmarked) require 2/3 regardless of who proposes them, or majority?

Arguments for 2/3 (Yes):
- Earmarked taxes bind future spending and impose on everyone; broad consensus justified.
- Consistency and anti-circumvention: Otherwise local officials can collude with allies to run "citizen" initiatives at low-turnout special elections, dodging both the 2/3 requirement AND the general-election timing requirement. (Upland also held initiatives can go on special election ballots.) This is a real governance concern: strategic timing + majority threshold = easy tax passage without broad consent. Though the initiative process itself requires signature gathering.
- Restores what voters intended in 1978/1996.
- Protects taxpayers/affordability in a high-cost, high-tax state.

Arguments for majority (No):
- One person, one vote; a tax approved by 60% of the people is democratically legitimate. Requiring 2/3 lets 1/3 impose its will — the opposite of majority rule — and empirically entrenches the status quo (which post-Prop 13 underfunds local services).
- Local self-determination: communities know their needs (wildfire protection in Sonoma, homelessness in LA).
- The signature requirement + majority election is itself a high bar; there's no evidence of rampant abuse.
- Fiscal needs: LAO notes revenues will be lower; with federal Medicaid cuts and state deficits, local safety nets need funding.
- Real-world examples of measures that would have failed: fire protection, homelessness services, healthcare.
- Even the author urges No; the measure is a hostage-exchange artifact, not considered policy. And the ballot title itself: "Limits Voters' Ability to Raise Revenues for Local Government Services."
- Money behind it: CA Business Roundtable (Thiel, Schmidt as top donors) — $10.69M; real estate/anti-ULA interests. Hmm wait, actually Thiel and Schmidt being top donors of the CA Business Roundtable Issues PAC is interesting but that PAC supports multiple things. Let me not overweight that.

Also consider the counterargument that the No side is heavily union-funded ($7.9M) — public employee unions benefit from local tax revenue. So both sides have interested money.

Neutral-ish observers: 
- SPUR: No.
- Press Democrat: No ("Prop. 43 wants to fix a system that isn't broken"; "The system, admittedly, is strange, but it works.")
- Santa Cruz Sentinel: No with reservations.
- Sac Bee: Yes ("Close ballot-box taxing loophole").
- Mercury News/East Bay Times (BANG): Yes ("Back Prop. 43 to restore voter-approved restrictions on local taxes").
- Southern California News Group (Daily Bulletin etc.): Yes.
- League of Women Voters? Let me check. California League of Cities? CSAC (counties) — presumably No. Let me check LWV and other good-government groups.

Let me also check what the LA Times editorial board said (they had a guide; did they endorse?). And the SF Chronicle. And the San Diego Union-Tribune. Also check PPIC poll (October) on Prop 43.

Also, I should think about the "which is better" question from the perspective of overall welfare and governance:

My assessment of the strongest points:

1. On pure democratic principle: majority rule should be the default for local self-taxation. The people voting to tax themselves — via initiative — is direct democracy at its most legitimate. A 2/3 requirement means a 66.6% supermajority is needed, i.e., 33.4% can veto. For a state constitutional amendment to permanently disable this local democratic tool statewide seems like overkill for addressing the "loophole" problem.

2. The loophole/circumvention concern is real but can be addressed more narrowly (e.g., requiring initiatives to appear at general elections, or requiring that government-backed "citizen" initiatives meet the 2/3 bar). Instead, Prop 43 applies 2/3 to ALL citizen-initiated special taxes, including genuine grassroots ones (e.g., Sonoma fire protection). The measure is a blunt instrument.

3. Empirical effect: It will block many majority-supported local revenue measures for essential services. In a state with chronic local fiscal stress (post-Prop 13), and with federal cuts, this will predictably worsen service funding. The LAO's fiscal note confirms the direction (lower revenues).

4. Taxpayer protection argument: California taxes are high in some respects, and the cost of living is brutal. But the answer to high taxes should be prioritization/spending reform, not structurally disabling local majorities from funding fire departments. Also note that general taxes (majority-vote, but must be at general elections and are unearmarked) remain available to local governments placed by councils; the citizen special tax initiative was one of the few ways communities could earmark for specific priorities. Under Prop 43, the option remains but at 2/3 — historically very hard (though not impossible; e.g., many 2/3 measures do pass, particularly parcel taxes in affluent areas).

Hmm, wait — but I should also consider: is there something to the idea that the 2/3 threshold "ensures broad consensus" and that many special taxes do pass at 2/3? Yes — in wealthy, liberal areas, parcel taxes routinely get 67-75%. But statewide, the pass rate at 2/3 is much lower. E.g., data from California City Finance/Edwin Park: special tax measures (2/3) pass around 50-60% of the time, vs general taxes (majority) ~80%+.

5. The "it's a deal/truce" argument for Yes: If Prop 43 fails, HJTA revives its initiative for 2028, which could be worse (retroactive repeals, broader 2/3 on fees, etc.). But: (a) the CA Supreme Court in Padilla (2024) already showed willingness to strike the broader version as an unconstitutional revision; (b) a future initiative would need to pass a statewide vote — uncertain; (c) accepting permanent policy you think is bad to avoid a hypothetical worse policy is a questionable trade; (d) in fact, Wicks and others calculate that voting No and fighting later is better. Also, the truce already achieved its main purpose (removing the 2026 HJTA initiative); a No vote doesn't restore it.

Hmm, but actually, let me reconsider: is the concern that HJTA's withdrawn initiative "would have devastated revenues for local governments and retroactively rescinded some local tax increases" — and if Prop 43 fails, HJTA will qualify it for 2028 and might win? Prop 43's own polling shows it trailing (No leading by ~10). A 2028 HJTA initiative would face similar headwinds but with different framing ("Taxpayer Protection Act") might pass. Uncertain.

6. There's also a fairness/consistency argument the other way: Why should a city council's special tax need 2/3 but a citizens' identical special tax need only majority? Two responses: (i) The initiative power is a constitutional right held by the people, and constraining it requires clear language (the Upland reasoning — courts won't construe statutes/constitutional provisions to limit the initiative power absent clarity); (ii) the asymmetry could also be fixed by lowering the government-proposed threshold... but that would require voter approval too and nobody proposed it. Given only one option is on the ballot, the question is whether the asymmetry as it stands is so harmful that it must be closed in the restrictive direction.

Actually, here's a subtle point: the practical "circumvention" is that city councils and mayors support "citizen" initiatives to get their preferred taxes through at majority. Examples: LA ULA had active support from councilmembers? Actually ULA was pushed by unions/housing groups; the city attorney put it on the ballot after signatures were verified. SF Prop C 2018 — Benioff-backed, opposed by the mayor and Board of Supervisors initially? Actually supervisors eventually supported? Not sure. LA County Measure A 2024 — was pushed by initiative (United Way, service providers) after Measure H (2/3, 69.5% in 2017) was set to expire; the county supported it. So yes, there's a pattern: when advocates know they can't hit 2/3 with a council-placed measure, they gather signatures for a majority-vote initiative. That IS a workaround of Prop 218's intent.

But is that workaround bad for the public? The workaround still requires a majority of voters to approve. Prop 218's 2/3 requirement for special taxes was itself a 1996 initiative (Howard Jarvis Association) that constrained local government. The "intent" of Prop 218's drafters was 2/3 for special taxes; but the language they wrote said "no local government may impose... approved by a two-thirds vote." The court read that literally. One can argue the drafters' sloppy language shouldn't be rescued at the expense of the initiative power.

From a voter's perspective in 2026: Do I want my community to be able to enact earmarked local taxes by majority vote via initiative? If yes → vote No on 43. Do I want broad consensus (2/3) for any tax? → vote Yes.

My own judgment: I find the No position more persuasive, primarily because:

(a) The anti-majoritarian structure of supermajority requirements is a strong democratic objection, especially for taxes that a community imposes on itself by direct vote. The "protection" being offered is protection from one's own majority — the people are the taxpayers.

(b) The practical consequences — blocking funding for fire, emergency response, homelessness, healthcare, housing that 55-66% of local voters support — are significant and negative for public welfare, particularly in an era of federal retrenchment. LA County Measure A (homelessness sales tax, ~$1.1B/yr) passed with ~53%... wait, hmm, would Measure A have passed at 2/3? No. So without the initiative route, LA County would have lost Measure H replacement funding. That's a big deal given the homelessness crisis.

Hold on — one consideration: maybe voters in a community SHOULD need 2/3 to impose earmarked taxes because earmarking constrains fiscal flexibility and because taxes fall on everyone (including the 47% minority). But the general tax (majority-vote) route already exists for councils; earmarking is a feature (accountability), not a bug. Requiring 2/3 for accountability-enhancing earmarks while allowing majority for general taxes creates weird incentives (governments just do general taxes and promise to spend on X — less enforceable).

(c) The measure is a permanent constitutional change crafted as a political bargain, opposed by its own author, and its ballot-case in favor rests on some questionable claims (e.g., the "bait-and-switch"/spending guarantee claim isn't actually in the text; the "2,000 new taxes" figure conflates general and special taxes; the "6% transfer tax" claim is about Oakland's... actually Oakland's transfer tax is 1.5%? The 6% figure refers to... Berkeley? No. Culver City's mansion tax (Measure BL?)? Actually, "Some cities now charge real estate transfer taxes as high as 6%" — hmm, that might refer to SF's commercial transfer tax tiers? No... Let me think: Santa Fe? In CA, Oakland charges 1.5%; SF up to 6% for properties over $25M! Yes, SF's transfer tax reaches 6% for $25M+ transactions (that's the top tier). So the claim is about SF's existing tax — not a new "loophole" creation. Actually SF's Prop C 2018 and Prop W... The pro argument's use is a bit misleading: SF's tiered transfer tax has existed for years (top tier added via 2020's Prop... the tiers went up to 5.5% or 6% for $25M+ after a 2020 ballot measure? Hmm. Berkeley Measure P (2018)? No. Anyway.)

(d) Editorial split: some credible papers say Yes (Sac Bee, BANG), some say No (Press Democrat, Santa Cruz Sentinel). The polling shows the public leaning No.

(e) SPUR (a respected urban policy think tank) says No. League of Women Voters of California — let me check. I believe LWVC is No. Let me verify quickly. Also California Teachers Association, firefighters, nurses — No. Chambers of commerce (Cal Chamber?) — Yes presumably. Let me check CalChamber's position — they usually do "job killer" lists. Not needed.

Let me do one more round of research: (1) LWVC position, (2) more details on the number of affected measures (e.g., an analysis of how many citizen-initiated special taxes passed 2018-2026 with 50-66%), (3) maybe the LA Times editorial board position, (4) PPIC October poll numbers on Prop 43, (5) the history of the HJTA deal (Politico/CalMatters coverage of ACA 22 passage and the withdrawn initiative 25-0006A1), to confirm the strategic dynamics.

Schaben, Los Angeles Times via Getty Images In summary The measure would require two-thirds of voters to approve any local special taxes, instead of the simple majority for citizen-led initiatives. Anti-tax advocates say it should be that hard for governments to tax Californians, but local officials say it could constrain funding for essential services. Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called. In 2022, 58% of Los Angeles city voters approved a hefty tax on mansion sales. In 2024, 62% of Sonoma County voters backed a half-cent sales tax to fund wildfire response and other emergency services. Neither would have become law under the threshold set by Proposition 43 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-43-tax-threshold/), which would require a two-thirds vote to pass any local tax measures that pay for specific services. Anti-tax advocates such as the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, which helped get Prop. 43 on the ballot, say it should be harder (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/08/california-constitution-proposition-43-taxes/) to tax Californians in a state where tax rates are already high. They argue that the measure would apply an equal standard to whoever wants a special tax, whether the government or citizen groups. Californians voted in 1996 (https://lao.ca.gov/1996/120196_prop_218/understanding_prop218_1296.html) to establish a two-thirds threshold for special tax measures. For decades, it was widely assumed that the threshold applied to all special taxes — until 2017, when the state Supreme Court said (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2017/08/state-supreme-court-made-easier-raise-taxes/) the law specifically applied only to tax measures put on the ballot by local officials. But what about special taxes proposed by citizens? The court declined to clarify (https://calmatters.org/economy/2019/02/local-tax-chaos-california-supreme-court/). Confusion ensued. Since then, several high-profile local special tax measures placed on the ballot by nongovernmental groups have passed with a simple majority. Local government officials, labor unions and affordable housing advocates oppose the measure, arguing the proposal would make it difficult to collect revenues for essential services, such as firefighting, education and healthcare. They argue it would allow “minority rule (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/08/proposition-43-taxes-minority-rule/)” because it would only take a third of voters to block special taxes. Jon Coupal, president of the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, said Prop. 43 would clarify that the two-thirds rule applies to all special taxes. He said that the two-thirds vote requirement dates to the 1849 state Constitution, which required a supermajority vote of state lawmakers to ask voters to borrow money. “The power to tax is (the) government’s most draconian power,” he told CalMatters. “The people of the state of California have made it a policy that when you are going to exercise that power, it should require a higher degree of consensus.” But opponents say the initiative risks kneecapping funding for local services. Darrell Roberts, president of the California Professional Firefighters union, which represents 38,000 firefighters, called Prop. 43 an insurmountable roadblock (https://www.marinij.com/2026/10/03/opinion-prop-43-sacrifices-local-public-safety-to-protect-corporate-profits/) to raising money for community services. This November, Los Angeles voters will decide on a half-cent sales tax (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-06/lapd-union-will-oppose-half-cent-sales-tax-hike-pushed-by-firefighters-union) proposal to hire more firefighters, Roberts noted. “Under Prop. 43, it’s clear that the powerful few would be protected at the expense of everyone else,” he wrote in the Marin Independent Journal. Supporters have poured almost $15 million into the measure, nearly $10 million of it from the California Business Roundtable PAC. Opponents have collected $6 million, with the biggest contribution, $1.5 million, from a PAC affiliated with the Service Employees International Union of California. Sign up for free Δ Prop. 43 originated from L.A.’s ‘mansion tax’ fight Prop. 43 stems from a bitter fight over Los Angeles’ “mansion tax,” a 4% tax on real estate sales of more than $5.3 million and 5.5% on sales more than $10.6 million. The tax rates rise with inflation. It has generated $1.4 billion (https://housing.lacity.gov/ula-revenue) in revenue since it became law in 2023, according to the city. The tax angered real estate developers (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/04/proposition-realty-mansion-tax-jarvis/) and business groups, who said it impeded new construction of all kinds of developments, including affordable housing. The opposition fueled a campaign led by Coupal’s group earlier this year to qualify a ballot measure that would have slashed real estate sales taxes statewide, applied the two-thirds vote requirement to all special taxes and revoked taxes that previously passed by a simple majority, such as the mansion tax. Prop. 43 is a more modest proposal resulting from an eleventh-hour negotiation between Coupal and Democratic leaders in the state Legislature to kill the more extensive version. Assemblymember Buffy Wicks (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/buffy-wicks-165044), an Oakland Democrat, authored the compromise language (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260aca22). The measure is limited to the vote threshold and does not apply retroactively to taxes such as the mansion tax. Just days after the Legislature placed Prop. 43 on the ballot, Wicks said she is “adamantly opposed” to it. “The clock was running out, and we had a choice to make: Leave a retroactive measure on the ballot that threatened billions in local funding, or accept a much narrower constitutional amendment that I still believed was bad policy,” Wicks said (https://bsky.app/profile/buffywicks.bsky.social/post/3mpi3t4tkmp2h) in a social media post. Is there public appetite? This isn’t Coupal’s first rodeo. In 2024, his group sponsored a much broader ballot measure to make it harder to raise taxes, but the California Supreme Court unanimously blocked (https://calmatters.org/politics/2024/06/california-taxes-supreme-court-ballot/) it before the election, deeming it an illegal attempt to change the state’s constitution. How will a narrower Prop. 43 perform this year? A September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) from the nonpartisan Public Policy Institute of California found 51% of likely voters would vote no on Prop. 43, versus just 43% who would vote yes. But Coupal hopes the proposal taps into voters’ concerns about affordability and their frustration with the high cost of living in California. “We are in a general climate right now where Californians really feel overtaxed,” he said. “California needs to prioritize its spending before it asks for more.” READ NEXT Why are out-of-state billionaires funding a California voter ID measure? Prop. 43 would make special taxes harder to pass. That’s the point, say anti-tax advocates

By Yue Stella Yu, CalMatters

This story was originally published by CalMatters. Sign up for their newsletters.

In 2022, 58% of Los Angeles city voters approved a hefty tax on mansion sales.

In 2024, 62% of Sonoma County voters backed a half-cent sales tax to fund wildfire response and other emergency services.

Neither would have become law under the threshold set by Proposition 43, which would require a two-thirds vote to pass any local tax measures that pay for specific services. 

Anti-tax advocates such as the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, which helped get Prop. 43 on the ballot, say it should be harder to tax Californians in a state where tax rates are already high. They argue that the measure would apply an equal standard to whoever wants a special tax, whether the government or citizen groups.

Californians voted in 1996 to establish a two-thirds threshold for special tax measures. For decades, it was widely assumed that the threshold applied to all special taxes — until 2017, when the state Supreme Court said the law specifically applied only to tax measures put on the ballot by local officials. 

But what about special taxes proposed by citizens? The court declined to clarify. Confusion ensued. Since then, several high-profile local special tax measures placed on the ballot by nongovernmental groups have passed with a simple majority.

Local government officials, labor unions and affordable housing advocates oppose the measure, arguing the proposal would make it difficult to collect revenues for essential services, such as firefighting, education and healthcare. Schaben, Los Angeles Times via Getty Images In summary The measure would require two-thirds of voters to approve any local special taxes, instead of the simple majority for citizen-led initiatives. Anti-tax advocates say it should be that hard for governments to tax Californians, but local officials say it could constrain funding for essential services. Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called. In 2022, 58% of Los Angeles city voters approved a hefty tax on mansion sales. In 2024, 62% of Sonoma County voters backed a half-cent sales tax to fund wildfire response and other emergency services. Neither would have become law under the threshold set by Proposition 43 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-43-tax-threshold/), which would require a two-thirds vote to pass any local tax measures that pay for specific services. Anti-tax advocates such as the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, which helped get Prop. 43 on the ballot, say it should be harder (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/08/california-constitution-proposition-43-taxes/) to tax Californians in a state where tax rates are already high. They argue that the measure would apply an equal standard to whoever wants a special tax, whether the government or citizen groups. Californians voted in 1996 (https://lao.ca.gov/1996/120196_prop_218/understanding_prop218_1296.html) to establish a two-thirds threshold for special tax measures. For decades, it was widely assumed that the threshold applied to all special taxes — until 2017, when the state Supreme Court said (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2017/08/state-supreme-court-made-easier-raise-taxes/) the law specifically applied only to tax measures put on the ballot by local officials. But what about special taxes proposed by citizens? The court declined to clarify (https://calmatters.org/economy/2019/02/local-tax-chaos-california-supreme-court/). Confusion ensued. Since then, several high-profile local special tax measures placed on the ballot by nongovernmental groups have passed with a simple majority. Local government officials, labor unions and affordable housing advocates oppose the measure, arguing the proposal would make it difficult to collect revenues for essential services, such as firefighting, education and healthcare. They argue it would allow “minority rule (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/08/proposition-43-taxes-minority-rule/)” because it would only take a third of voters to block special taxes. Jon Coupal, president of the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, said Prop. 43 would clarify that the two-thirds rule applies to all special taxes. He said that the two-thirds vote requirement dates to the 1849 state Constitution, which required a supermajority vote of state lawmakers to ask voters to borrow money. “The power to tax is (the) government’s most draconian power,” he told CalMatters. “The people of the state of California have made it a policy that when you are going to exercise that power, it should require a higher degree of consensus.” But opponents say the initiative risks kneecapping funding for local services. Darrell Roberts, president of the California Professional Firefighters union, which represents 38,000 firefighters, called Prop. 43 an insurmountable roadblock (https://www.marinij.com/2026/10/03/opinion-prop-43-sacrifices-local-public-safety-to-protect-corporate-profits/) to raising money for community services. This November, Los Angeles voters will decide on a half-cent sales tax (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-06/lapd-union-will-oppose-half-cent-sales-tax-hike-pushed-by-firefighters-union) proposal to hire more firefighters, Roberts noted. “Under Prop. 43, it’s clear that the powerful few would be protected at the expense of everyone else,” he wrote in the Marin Independent Journal. Supporters have poured almost $15 million into the measure, nearly $10 million of it from the California Business Roundtable PAC. Opponents have collected $6 million, with the biggest contribution, $1.5 million, from a PAC affiliated with the Service Employees International Union of California. Sign up for free Δ Prop. 43 originated from L.A.’s ‘mansion tax’ fight Prop. 43 stems from a bitter fight over Los Angeles’ “mansion tax,” a 4% tax on real estate sales of more than $5.3 million and 5.5% on sales more than $10.6 million. The tax rates rise with inflation. It has generated $1.4 billion (https://housing.lacity.gov/ula-revenue) in revenue since it became law in 2023, according to the city. The tax angered real estate developers (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/04/proposition-realty-mansion-tax-jarvis/) and business groups, who said it impeded new construction of all kinds of developments, including affordable housing. The opposition fueled a campaign led by Coupal’s group earlier this year to qualify a ballot measure that would have slashed real estate sales taxes statewide, applied the two-thirds vote requirement to all special taxes and revoked taxes that previously passed by a simple majority, such as the mansion tax. Prop. 43 is a more modest proposal resulting from an eleventh-hour negotiation between Coupal and Democratic leaders in the state Legislature to kill the more extensive version. Assemblymember Buffy Wicks (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/buffy-wicks-165044), an Oakland Democrat, authored the compromise language (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260aca22). The measure is limited to the vote threshold and does not apply retroactively to taxes such as the mansion tax. Just days after the Legislature placed Prop. 43 on the ballot, Wicks said she is “adamantly opposed” to it. “The clock was running out, and we had a choice to make: Leave a retroactive measure on the ballot that threatened billions in local funding, or accept a much narrower constitutional amendment that I still believed was bad policy,” Wicks said (https://bsky.app/profile/buffywicks.bsky.social/post/3mpi3t4tkmp2h) in a social media post. Is there public appetite? This isn’t Coupal’s first rodeo. In 2024, his group sponsored a much broader ballot measure to make it harder to raise taxes, but the California Supreme Court unanimously blocked (https://calmatters.org/politics/2024/06/california-taxes-supreme-court-ballot/) it before the election, deeming it an illegal attempt to change the state’s constitution. How will a narrower Prop. 43 perform this year? A September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) from the nonpartisan Public Policy Institute of California found 51% of likely voters would vote no on Prop. 43, versus just 43% who would vote yes. But Coupal hopes the proposal taps into voters’ concerns about affordability and their frustration with the high cost of living in California. “We are in a general climate right now where Californians really feel overtaxed,” he said. “California needs to prioritize its spending before it asks for more.” READ NEXT Why are out-of-state billionaires funding a California voter ID measure? Anti-tax advocates say it should be that hard for governments to tax Californians, but local officials say it could constrain funding for essential services. In 2022, 58% of Los Angeles city voters approved a hefty tax on mansion sales. In 2024, 62% of Sonoma County voters backed a half-cent sales tax to fund wildfire response and other emergency services. Neither would have become law under the threshold set by Proposition 43 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-43-tax-threshold/), which would require a two-thirds vote to pass any local tax measures that pay for specific services. Anti-tax advocates such as the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, which helped get Prop. 43 on the ballot, say it should be harder (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/08/california-constitution-proposition-43-taxes/) to tax Californians in a state where tax rates are already high. They argue that the measure would apply an equal standard to whoever wants a special tax, whether the government or citizen groups. Californians voted in 1996 (https://lao.ca.gov/1996/120196_prop_218/understanding_prop218_1296.html) to establish a two-thirds threshold for special tax measures. For decades, it was widely assumed that the threshold applied to all special taxes — until 2017, when the state Supreme Court said (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2017/08/state-supreme-court-made-easier-raise-taxes/) the law specifically applied only to tax measures put on the ballot by local officials. But what about special taxes proposed by citizens? The court declined to clarify (https://calmatters.org/economy/2019/02/local-tax-chaos-california-supreme-court/). Confusion ensued. Since then, several high-profile local special tax measures placed on the ballot by nongovernmental groups have passed with a simple majority. Local government officials, labor unions and affordable housing advocates oppose the measure, arguing the proposal would make it difficult to collect revenues for essential services, such as firefighting, education and healthcare. They argue it would allow “minority rule (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/08/proposition-43-taxes-minority-rule/)” because it would only take a third of voters to block special taxes. Jon Coupal, president of the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, said Prop. 43 would clarify that the two-thirds rule applies to all special taxes. He said that the two-thirds vote requirement dates to the 1849 state Constitution, which required a supermajority vote of state lawmakers to ask voters to borrow money. “The power to tax is (the) government’s most draconian power,” he told CalMatters. “The people of the state of California have made it a policy that when you are going to exercise that power, it should require a higher degree of consensus.” But opponents say the initiative risks kneecapping funding for local services. Darrell Roberts, president of the California Professional Firefighters union, which represents 38,000 firefighters, called Prop. 43 an insurmountable roadblock (https://www.marinij.com/2026/10/03/opinion-prop-43-sacrifices-local-public-safety-to-protect-corporate-profits/) to raising money for community services. This November, Los Angeles voters will decide on a half-cent sales tax (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-06/lapd-union-will-oppose-half-cent-sales-tax-hike-pushed-by-firefighters-union) proposal to hire more firefighters, Roberts noted. “Under Prop. 43, it’s clear that the powerful few would be protected at the expense of everyone else,” he wrote in the Marin Independent Journal. Supporters have poured almost $15 million into the measure, nearly $10 million of it from the California Business Roundtable PAC. Opponents have collected $6 million, with the biggest contribution, $1.5 million, from a PAC affiliated with the Service Employees International Union of California. Sign up for free Δ Prop. 43 originated from L.A.’s ‘mansion tax’ fight Prop. 43 stems from a bitter fight over Los Angeles’ “mansion tax,” a 4% tax on real estate sales of more than $5.3 million and 5.5% on sales more than $10.6 million. The tax rates rise with inflation. It has generated $1.4 billion (https://housing.lacity.gov/ula-revenue) in revenue since it became law in 2023, according to the city. The tax angered real estate developers (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/04/proposition-realty-mansion-tax-jarvis/) and business groups, who said it impeded new construction of all kinds of developments, including affordable housing. The opposition fueled a campaign led by Coupal’s group earlier this year to qualify a ballot measure that would have slashed real estate sales taxes statewide, applied the two-thirds vote requirement to all special taxes and revoked taxes that previously passed by a simple majority, such as the mansion tax. Prop. 43 is a more modest proposal resulting from an eleventh-hour negotiation between Coupal and Democratic leaders in the state Legislature to kill the more extensive version. Assemblymember Buffy Wicks (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/buffy-wicks-165044), an Oakland Democrat, authored the compromise language (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260aca22). The measure is limited to the vote threshold and does not apply retroactively to taxes such as the mansion tax. Just days after the Legislature placed Prop. 43 on the ballot, Wicks said she is “adamantly opposed” to it. “The clock was running out, and we had a choice to make: Leave a retroactive measure on the ballot that threatened billions in local funding, or accept a much narrower constitutional amendment that I still believed was bad policy,” Wicks said (https://bsky.app/profile/buffywicks.bsky.social/post/3mpi3t4tkmp2h) in a social media post. Is there public appetite? This isn’t Coupal’s first rodeo. In 2024, his group sponsored a much broader ballot measure to make it harder to raise taxes, but the California Supreme Court unanimously blocked (https://calmatters.org/politics/2024/06/california-taxes-supreme-court-ballot/) it before the election, deeming it an illegal attempt to change the state’s constitution. How will a narrower Prop. 43 perform this year? A September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) from the nonpartisan Public Policy Institute of California found 51% of likely voters would vote no on Prop. 43, versus just 43% who would vote yes. But Coupal hopes the proposal taps into voters’ concerns about affordability and their frustration with the high cost of living in California. “We are in a general climate right now where Californians really feel overtaxed,” he said. “California needs to prioritize its spending before it asks for more.” READ NEXT Why are out-of-state billionaires funding a California voter ID measure? #### LIMITS VOTERS’ ABILITY TO RAISE REVENUES FOR LOCAL GOVERNMENT SERVICES
Prop 43 would make it harder for communities to raise revenue for public services by allowing a minority of voters to block local tax measures.
It would amend the Constitution to require a two-thirds vote for any new, increased, or extended special tax proposed by local voters through the initiative process.
A simple majority keeps these decisions with most voters and gives communities more flexibility to respond to changing needs.
