Now I have the actual text of Prop 43. It's quite short:

"SEC. 4.5. (a) Beginning on January 1, 2027, and notwithstanding Article II and Article XI, no local government, including the electorate of a local government exercising the initiative power, may impose, extend, or increase any special tax, except as provided in Section 4 of this article [Art XIII A Sec 4 - ad valorem property tax rates], subdivision (d) of Section 2 of Article XIII C [the existing 2/3 requirement for government-imposed special taxes], and paragraph (2) of subdivision (a) of Section 3 of Article XIII D, unless and until that tax is submitted to the electorate and approved by a two-thirds vote.
(b) Notwithstanding Article II and Article XI, no local government, including the electorate of a local government exercising the initiative power, may impose ad valorem taxes on real property, except as provided in paragraph (1) of subdivision (a) of Section XIII D.
(c) 'Local government' and 'special tax' shall have the same meaning as provided in Section 1 of Article XIII C."

Interesting: note that the pro argument claimed Prop 43 "requires governments to spend tax revenue for the specific purpose voters approved" — I don't see that in the text. That's arguably a misleading claim in the ballot argument (the "bait-and-switch" claim). Special taxes by definition are earmarked... Actually, Prop 218 Article XIII D already requires special taxes to be used for the specific purpose. Whatever.

Also interesting: Section (b) prohibits ad valorem real property taxes via initiative except as permitted under Art XIII D 3(a)(1) — which relates to... Article XIII D section 3(a) says no fee may be imposed on a parcel... Hmm, actually Art. XIII D 3(a)(1) concerns special assessments? Let me not go too deep. The key: it prevents local voters from using initiatives to impose new property taxes beyond existing constitutional limits (e.g., "split roll"-lite or parcel-like ad valorem taxes).

Key context on the deal: The Berkeley city council document (Igor Tregub item) mentions: "Initiative 25-0006A1, titled the 'Local Taxpayer Protection Act to Save Proposition 13,' was submitted and received the signatures necessary to qualify for placement on the [ballot]..." — this is the HJTA initiative that was withdrawn as part of the deal in exchange for ACA 22 (Prop 43).

Also the CalMatters piece: "Democratic legislators and Newsom were removed as supporters of Proposition 43, after they brokered the deal to put it on the ballot." And Wicks, the author, now urges No.

Polling: Berkeley IGS September: Yes 31 / No 40 / Undecided 29. Late October: Yes 36 / No 46. So it's trailing.

Now let me think about the substantive merits more carefully, since the user wants me to do extensive research and come to a decision.

Let me gather a bit more on: (1) how many local measures would be affected / have passed below 2/3 (e.g., Measure A LA County 2024 homelessness sales tax — passed with ~53%? Actually LA County Measure A (Nov 2024) passed with ~53.2%? Let me check. It replaced Measure H (2017, 2/3, passed with 69.5%?). Hmm, Measure A was a citizen's initiative? I believe Measure A 2024 was placed on the ballot via initiative by homeless advocates (united way etc.) precisely to use the majority-vote route. It passed with about 53-54%. Under Prop 43, it would have failed. Also Berkeley Measure P (2018, soda tax), Oakland soda taxes (2016), SF Prop C (2018, 61%), Prop W... Albany, Richmond... These soda taxes were citizen initiatives passing ~50-70%. Berkeley Measure O (2020)? Culver City? Also SF's Prop C (2018, homeless services tax on corporations, 61%) — passed via initiative after Board of Supervisors couldn't put it at 2/3? Actually SF Prop C (2018) was placed by signature... it was backed by Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff, qualified via signatures, passed 60.9%. SF later passed Prop M (2024) restructuring...

Also there were 2020-2024 examples: Monterey County Measure...? Humboldt? Mendocino? Various school parcel taxes (those are gov-proposed, 2/3). The citizen-initiative route has been used in: SF (Prop C 2018, Prop W 2018 free city college), Oakland (2020 Measure Q parks... passed 53%?; Measure S homeless?; Measure T?; Measure U oakland affordable housing 2021, 67.7%? passed just above 2/3), LA (Measure ULA 2022, 57.8%), LA County (Measure A 2024, ~53%), Culver City 2024...? El Monte, Santa Cruz (Measure C 2025?), Santa Clara County (Measure A 2025), Sonoma (Measure H 2024, 62%)... wait, Sonoma Measure H was described by CalMatters: "In 2024, 62% of Sonoma County voters backed a half-cent sales tax to fund wildfire response and other emergency services." Was it citizen-initiated? Probably yes (or extended existing?). Anyway.

So the practical effect: a bunch of major revenue measures — LA County Measure A (homelessness, ~$1B/yr), LA City ULA (~$300-900M/yr intended), SF Prop C 2018 (~$300M/yr), etc. — passed with 53-62% and would have failed under 2/3. Under Prop 43, all future such measures would need 2/3.

The Yes side says: that's the point — these taxes were enacted without the constitutionally required broad support; courts eroded Prop 13/218.

Now, the fundamental policy question: Should special taxes (earmarked) require 2/3 regardless of who proposes them, or majority?

Arguments for 2/3 (Yes):
- Earmarked taxes bind future spending and impose on everyone; broad consensus justified.
- Consistency and anti-circumvention: Otherwise local officials can collude with allies to run "citizen" initiatives at low-turnout special elections, dodging both the 2/3 requirement AND the general-election timing requirement. (Upland also held initiatives can go on special election ballots.) This is a real governance concern: strategic timing + majority threshold = easy tax passage without broad consent. Though the initiative process itself requires signature gathering.
- Restores what voters intended in 1978/1996.
- Protects taxpayers/affordability in a high-cost, high-tax state.

Arguments for majority (No):
- One person, one vote; a tax approved by 60% of the people is democratically legitimate. Requiring 2/3 lets 1/3 impose its will — the opposite of majority rule — and empirically entrenches the status quo (which post-Prop 13 underfunds local services).
- Local self-determination: communities know their needs (wildfire protection in Sonoma, homelessness in LA).
- The signature requirement + majority election is itself a high bar; there's no evidence of rampant abuse.
- Fiscal needs: LAO notes revenues will be lower; with federal Medicaid cuts and state deficits, local safety nets need funding.
- Real-world examples of measures that would have failed: fire protection, homelessness services, healthcare.
- Even the author urges No; the measure is a hostage-exchange artifact, not considered policy. And the ballot title itself: "Limits Voters' Ability to Raise Revenues for Local Government Services."
- Money behind it: CA Business Roundtable (Thiel, Schmidt as top donors) — $10.69M; real estate/anti-ULA interests. Hmm wait, actually Thiel and Schmidt being top donors of the CA Business Roundtable Issues PAC is interesting but that PAC supports multiple things. Let me not overweight that.

Also consider the counterargument that the No side is heavily union-funded ($7.9M) — public employee unions benefit from local tax revenue. So both sides have interested money.

Neutral-ish observers: 
- SPUR: No.

In 2022, 58% of Los Angeles city voters approved a hefty tax on mansion sales. In 2024, 62% of Sonoma County voters backed a half-cent sales tax to fund wildfire response and other emergency services. Neither would have become law under the threshold set by Proposition 43 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-43-tax-threshold/), which would require a two-thirds vote to pass any local tax measures that pay for specific services. Anti-tax advocates such as the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, which helped get Prop. 43 on the ballot, say it should be harder (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/08/california-constitution-proposition-43-taxes/) to tax Californians in a state where tax rates are already high. They argue that the measure would apply an equal standard to whoever wants a special tax, whether the government or citizen groups. Californians voted in 1996 (https://lao.ca.gov/1996/120196_prop_218/understanding_prop218_1296.html) to establish a two-thirds threshold for special tax measures. For decades, it was widely assumed that the threshold applied to all special taxes — until 2017, when the state Supreme Court said (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2017/08/state-supreme-court-made-easier-raise-taxes/) the law specifically applied only to tax measures put on the ballot by local officials. But what about special taxes proposed by citizens? The court declined to clarify (https://calmatters.org/economy/2019/02/local-tax-chaos-california-supreme-court/). Confusion ensued. Since then, several high-profile local special tax measures placed on the ballot by nongovernmental groups have passed with a simple majority. Local government officials, labor unions and affordable housing advocates oppose the measure, arguing the proposal would make it difficult to collect revenues for essential services, such as firefighting, education and healthcare. They argue it would allow “minority rule (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/08/proposition-43-taxes-minority-rule/)” because it would only take a third of voters to block special taxes. Jon Coupal, president of the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, said Prop. 43 would clarify that the two-thirds rule applies to all special taxes. He said that the two-thirds vote requirement dates to the 1849 state Constitution, which required a supermajority vote of state lawmakers to ask voters to borrow money. “The power to tax is (the) government’s most draconian power,” he told CalMatters. “The people of the state of California have made it a policy that when you are going to exercise that power, it should require a higher degree of consensus.” But opponents say the initiative risks kneecapping funding for local services. Darrell Roberts, president of the California Professional Firefighters union, which represents 38,000 firefighters, called Prop. 43 an insurmountable roadblock (https://www.marinij.com/2026/10/03/opinion-prop-43-sacrifices-local-public-safety-to-protect-corporate-profits/) to raising money for community services. This November, Los Angeles voters will decide on a half-cent sales tax (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-06/lapd-union-will-oppose-half-cent-sales-tax-hike-pushed-by-firefighters-union) proposal to hire more firefighters, Roberts noted. “Under Prop. 43, it’s clear that the powerful few would be protected at the expense of everyone else,” he wrote in the Marin Independent Journal. Supporters have poured almost $15 million into the measure, nearly $10 million of it from the California Business Roundtable PAC. Opponents have collected $6 million, with the biggest contribution, $1.5 million, from a PAC affiliated with the Service Employees International Union of California. Sign up for free Δ Prop. 43 originated from L.A.’s ‘mansion tax’ fight Prop. 43 stems from a bitter fight over Los Angeles’ “mansion tax,” a 4% tax on real estate sales of more than $5.3 million and 5.5% on sales more than $10.6 million. The tax rates rise with inflation. It has generated $1.4 billion (https://housing.lacity.gov/ula-revenue) in revenue since it became law in 2023, according to the city. The tax angered real estate developers (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/04/proposition-realty-mansion-tax-jarvis/) and business groups, who said it impeded new construction of all kinds of developments, including affordable housing. The opposition fueled a campaign led by Coupal’s group earlier this year to qualify a ballot measure that would have slashed real estate sales taxes statewide, applied the two-thirds vote requirement to all special taxes and revoked taxes that previously passed by a simple majority, such as the mansion tax. Prop. 43 is a more modest proposal resulting from an eleventh-hour negotiation between Coupal and Democratic leaders in the state Legislature to kill the more extensive version. Assemblymember Buffy Wicks (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/buffy-wicks-165044), an Oakland Democrat, authored the compromise language (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260aca22). The measure is limited to the vote threshold and does not apply retroactively to taxes such as the mansion tax. Just days after the Legislature placed Prop. 43 on the ballot, Wicks said she is “adamantly opposed” to it. “The clock was running out, and we had a choice to make: Leave a retroactive measure on the ballot that threatened billions in local funding, or accept a much narrower constitutional amendment that I still believed was bad policy,” Wicks said (https://bsky.app/profile/buffywicks.bsky.social/post/3mpi3t4tkmp2h) in a social media post. Is there public appetite? This isn’t Coupal’s first rodeo. In 2024, his group sponsored a much broader ballot measure to make it harder to raise taxes, but the California Supreme Court unanimously blocked (https://calmatters.org/politics/2024/06/california-taxes-supreme-court-ballot/) it before the election, deeming it an illegal attempt to change the state’s constitution. How will a narrower Prop. 43 perform this year? A September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) from the nonpartisan Public Policy Institute of California found 51% of likely voters would vote no on Prop. 43, versus just 43% who would vote yes. But Coupal hopes the proposal taps into voters’ concerns about affordability and their frustration with the high cost of living in California. “We are in a general climate right now where Californians really feel overtaxed,” he said. “California needs to prioritize its spending before it asks for more.” READ NEXT Why are out-of-state billionaires funding a California voter ID measure? Now I have a comprehensive picture. Let me consolidate:

**What Prop 43 does:**
- Constitutional amendment (ACA 22, Wicks; Res. Ch. 132, 2026), adds Section 4.5 to Article XIII A.
- Beginning Jan 1, 2027, any new/increased/extended local special tax proposed by voters (initiative) would require a two-thirds vote (same as government-proposed special taxes under Prop 218, Art. XIII C §2(d)).
- Also constitutionally bars local governments or local electorates (via initiative) from imposing ad valorem taxes on real property except as already permitted.
- Prospective only — doesn't retroactively repeal existing taxes like ULA or Measure A.

**Background:**
- Prop 13 (1978) and Prop 218 (1996) imposed 2/3 for special taxes "imposed by local government."
- California Cannabis Coalition v. City of Upland (2017, CA Supreme Court, 5-2): constitutional limits in Art. XIII C §2 apply to local governments, not voter initiatives. Subsequent Court of Appeal decisions (SF v. All Persons Interested in Prop C (2020), City of Fresno v. Fresno Building Healthy Communities (2020), HJTA v. SF (2020), Alzheimer's Society v. Menlo Park (2022)) allowed citizen-initiated special taxes by simple majority.
- Result: asymmetry — gov-proposed special taxes need 2/3; citizen-initiated need majority. Groups use the initiative route strategically (e.g., LA County Measure A 2024, 55.7%, ~$1.1B/yr for homelessness; LA City Measure ULA 2022, 57.8%, $1.4B generated since 2023; SF Prop C 2018, 61%, ~$300M/yr; Sonoma Measure H 2024, 62%).
- HJTA qualified a broader initiative (Initiative 25-0006A1, "Local Taxpayer Protection Act to Save Prop 13") that would have slashed transfer taxes, applied 2/3 to all special taxes, and retroactively revoked majority-passed taxes. Deal: Democrats (Wicks) put ACA 22 (narrower, prospective) on ballot; HJTA withdrew; Legislature also pulled its countermeasure ACA 13. Wicks herself says she is "adamantly opposed" to Prop 43 and urges No.
- In 2024, the CA Supreme Court blocked HJTA's broader TPGAA as an unconstitutional revision (Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Assn. v. Padilla).

**Fiscal effect (LAO):** Local revenues possibly lower in the future. No dollar estimate.

**Polling:** PPIC Sept: 43 yes / 51 no; Oct: 42 yes / 55 no. Berkeley IGS Sept: 31/40/29; late Oct: 36/46. Trailing.

**Positions:**
- Yes: HJTA, CalTaxpayers Assn, Family Business Assn, CA Hispanic Chambers, CA Small Business Assn, CA Consumer Advocates for Affordability and Safety, Cal Business Roundtable PAC ($10.7M; top donors Thiel/Schmidt), editorial boards: Sac Bee, Mercury News/East Bay Times, SoCal News Group (Daily Bulletin etc.).
- No: CA Professional Firefighters, CA Federation of Teachers, Nurse Alliance SEIU, CSEA, Californians Against Waste, Non-Profit Housing Assn, Sierra Business Council, AAPI Force, Communities for a Better Environment, League of Women Voters of California, SPUR, MidPen Housing, League of CA Cities/CSAC presumably, Becerra (gubernatorial candidate), Wicks (author); editorial boards: Press Democrat, Santa Cruz Sentinel; labor money ~$6-8M (SEIU).

**Substance weighing:**

Yes case (real merits):
- Uniform 2/3 standard for earmarked local taxes regardless of proposer; closes the circumvention strategy where officials/interest groups use signature campaigns to dodge 2/3 and general-election timing rules.
- Historically, the 2/3 rule was understood to apply to all special taxes from 1978-2017.
- Supermajority for taxes = consensus for government's "most draconian power" (Coupal).
- Protects affordability; prevents targeted taxes on real estate etc.
- The compromise avoided a retroactive, far more destructive measure; preserves the truce.

No case (real merits):
- Minority veto: 33.4% can block what up to 66.6% want — anti-majoritarian; LWV: "makes it harder for communities to raise revenue when local needs or economic conditions change."
- No tax cut; only blocks future locally-supported revenue for fire/EMS/schools/roads/healthcare/housing.
- Concrete major measures that would have failed: LA County Measure A (55.7%), LA ULA (57.8%), SF Prop C (61%), Sonoma fire tax (62%) — billions for homelessness, housing, fire.
- Local self-governance/direct democracy: the people ARE the taxpayers; a majority vote on self-taxation is legitimate consent.
- Permanent constitutional change; even its author says it's bad policy; it's a hostage bargain artifact.
- The No side's supporters include public safety, educators, nurses, LWV.

My decision. I've weighed both. Key judgment calls:

1. Is the asymmetry a "loophole" that must be closed by raising the citizen-initiative threshold to 2/3, or should majority rule be preserved for local voter self-taxation?

I keep coming back to: the people voting to tax themselves, by majority, is the essence of local democratic self-governance. The "loophole" framing presupposes that the 2/3 rule was intended to bind the people's own initiative power — but the courts held otherwise because the constitution's text says "no local government may impose." Moreover, the initiative route has a built-in check (signature qualification + election). The harms cited (low-turnout elections, "special interests") are speculative relative to the demonstrated, concrete harms of the 2/3 threshold (blocked funding for homelessness response, wildfire protection, etc.).

2. Practical consequences: The LAO itself frames the fiscal impact as "local government tax revenues will not go up as much." Given the state of local finances (federal cuts, deferred infrastructure, wildfire risk, homelessness crisis), making the citizen-initiative special tax route require 2/3 will predictably kill many future funding measures in the 55-66% range. The two-thirds rule for gov-proposed special taxes already exists as a (very high) bar; extending it to citizen initiatives forecloses the main remaining responsive tool.

3. Democratic principle: supermajority requirements for ordinary decisions entrench minority rule. California has plenty of taxpayer protections already (Prop 13 property limits, 2/3 for gov special taxes, 2/3 legislative vote for state tax increases, Gann limit). This measure adds a minority veto over community decisions.

4. The strategic "truce" argument for Yes is real but weak for a single voter: the worse retroactive initiative was already withdrawn and can't return in 2026; if it returns in 2028, voters can fight it then (and the Supreme Court has shown willingness to strike the most sweeping version as an invalid revision). Locking in a permanent constitutional minority veto now to buy temporary peace is a bad trade if the underlying policy is bad.

5. Editorial and civic-group weight: mixed on editorial boards (Bee/BANG/SCNG yes; Press Democrat/Santa Cruz no), but good-government/civic organizations (LWV, SPUR) and the author herself say No. Polls show the electorate leaning No (PPIC 55% no).

The user asked: "Is it better to vote yes or no on this prop? ... Answer with only `yes` or `no`."

So my final answer must be just the single word. Given my analysis, the answer is "no."

One more consideration — should I double check the SPUR reasoning and maybe the SF Chronicle/LA Times editorial positions to make sure I'm not missing a compelling Yes argument? I've seen the Yes arguments in full (ballot arguments + HJTA commentary + Bee/BANG editorials summarized). The Yes case boils down to: uniformity/loophole-closing, taxpayer protection, affordability. I've considered those. The No case: majority rule, local flexibility, service funding, no tax cut, permanent constitutional entrenchment, author opposes.

I'm comfortable with "No."

Actually, let me reflect once more on the strongest Yes argument to make sure I'm not underweighting it: "The system currently lets local officials collude with interest groups to impose taxes with 50%+1 at low-turnout special elections, dodging both the 2/3 threshold and the general-election timing requirement. This is a genuine circumvention of Prop 218's voter protections, and courts can't fix it; only a constitutional amendment can."

Response: (1) Signature-gathering is a significant hurdle that itself requires broad grassroots support; (2) the majority-vote requirement at the election is still a democratic check by the very taxpayers; (3) the problem could be addressed with narrower fixes (e.g., initiatives at general elections only); (4) empirically, the measures passed this way fund widely-shared services and were approved by majorities of 53-62% in high-turnout general elections mostly; (5) the cost of the fix (2/3 for everything) far exceeds the harm. Also the "6% transfer tax" and "2,000 new taxes" claims in the Yes argument are overstated/misleading (SF's 6% top-tier transfer tax predates and isn't a "loophole" creation; the 2,000 figure includes majority-vote general taxes and legally-passed 2/3 special taxes).

Now I have a comprehensive picture. Let me consolidate:

**What Prop 43 does:**
- Constitutional amendment (ACA 22, Wicks; Res. Ch. 132, 2026), adds Section 4.5 to Article XIII A.
- Beginning Jan 1, 2027, any new/increased/extended local special tax proposed by voters (initiative) would require a two-thirds vote (same as government-proposed special taxes under Prop 218, Art. XIII C §2(d)).
- Also constitutionally bars local governments or local electorates (via initiative) from imposing ad valorem taxes on real property except as already permitted.
- Prospective only — doesn't retroactively repeal existing taxes like ULA or Measure A.

**Background:**
- Prop 13 (1978) and Prop 218 (1996) imposed 2/3 for special taxes "imposed by local government."
- California Cannabis Coalition v. City of Upland (2017, CA Supreme Court, 5-2): constitutional limits in Art. XIII C §2 apply to local governments, not voter initiatives. Subsequent Court of Appeal decisions (SF v. All Persons Interested in Prop C (2020), City of Fresno v. Fresno Building Healthy Communities (2020), HJTA v. SF (2020), Alzheimer's Society v. Menlo Park (2022)) allowed citizen-initiated special taxes by simple majority.
- Result: asymmetry — gov-proposed special taxes need 2/3; citizen-initiated need majority. Groups use the initiative route strategically (e.g., LA County Measure A 2024, 55.7%, ~$1.1B/yr for homelessness; LA City Measure ULA 2022, 57.8%, $1.4B generated since 2023; SF Prop C 2018, 61%, ~$300M/yr; Sonoma Measure H 2024, 62%).
- HJTA qualified a broader initiative (Initiative 25-0006A1, "Local Taxpayer Protection Act to Save Prop 13") that would have slashed transfer taxes, applied 2/3 to all special taxes, and retroactively revoked majority-passed taxes. Deal: Democrats (Wicks) put ACA 22 (narrower, prospective) on ballot; HJTA withdrew; Legislature also pulled its countermeasure ACA 13. Wicks herself says she is "adamantly opposed" to Prop 43 and urges No.
- In 2024, the CA Supreme Court blocked HJTA's broader TPGAA as an unconstitutional revision (Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Assn. v. Padilla).

**Fiscal effect (LAO):** Local revenues possibly lower in the future. No dollar estimate.

**Polling:** PPIC Sept: 43 yes / 51 no; Oct: 42 yes / 55 no. Berkeley IGS Sept: 31/40/29; late Oct: 36/46. Trailing.

**Positions:**
- Yes: HJTA, CalTaxpayers Assn, Family Business Assn, CA Hispanic Chambers, CA Small Business Assn, CA Consumer Advocates for Affordability and Safety, Cal Business Roundtable PAC ($10.7M; top donors Thiel/Schmidt), editorial boards: Sac Bee, Mercury News/East Bay Times, SoCal News Group (Daily Bulletin etc.).
- No: CA Professional Firefighters, CA Federation of Teachers, Nurse Alliance SEIU, CSEA, Californians Against Waste, Non-Profit Housing Assn, Sierra Business Council, AAPI Force, Communities for a Better Environment, League of Women Voters of California, SPUR, MidPen Housing, League of CA Cities/CSAC presumably, Becerra (gubernatorial candidate), Wicks (author); editorial boards: Press Democrat, Santa Cruz Sentinel; labor money ~$6-8M (SEIU).

**Substance weighing:**

Yes case (real merits):
- Uniform 2/3 standard for earmarked local taxes regardless of proposer; closes the circumvention strategy where officials/interest groups use signature campaigns to dodge 2/3 and general-election timing rules.

- The compromise avoided a retroactive, far more destructive measure; preserves the truce.

No case (real merits):
- Minority veto: 33.4% can block what up to 66.6% want — anti-majoritarian; LWV: "makes it harder for communities to raise revenue when local needs or economic conditions change."
- No tax cut; only blocks future locally-supported revenue for fire/EMS/schools/roads/healthcare/housing.
- Concrete major measures that would have failed: LA County Measure A (55.7%), LA ULA (57.8%), SF Prop C (61%), Sonoma fire tax (62%) — billions for homelessness, housing, fire.

- Permanent constitutional change; even its author says it's bad policy; it's a hostage bargain artifact.
- The No side's supporters include public safety, educators, nurses, LWV.

My decision. I've weighed both. Key judgment calls:

1. Is the asymmetry a "loophole" that must be closed by raising the citizen-initiative threshold to 2/3, or should majority rule be preserved for local voter self-taxation?

Moreover, the initiative route has a built-in check (signature qualification + election). The two-thirds rule for gov-proposed special taxes already exists as a (very high) bar; extending it to citizen initiatives forecloses the main remaining responsive tool.

3. Democratic principle: supermajority requirements for ordinary decisions entrench minority rule. California has plenty of taxpayer protections already (Prop 13 property limits, 2/3 for gov special taxes, 2/3 legislative vote for state tax increases, Gann limit). - The compromise avoided a retroactive, far more destructive measure; preserves the truce.

No case (real merits):
- Minority veto: 33.4% can block what up to 66.6% want — anti-majoritarian; LWV: "makes it harder for communities to raise revenue when local needs or economic conditions change."
- No tax cut; only blocks future locally-supported revenue for fire/EMS/schools/roads/healthcare/housing.
- Concrete major measures that would have failed: LA County Measure A (55.7%), LA ULA (57.8%), SF Prop C (61%), Sonoma fire tax (62%) — billions for homelessness, housing, fire.
- Local self-governance/direct democracy: the people ARE the taxpayers; a majority vote on self-taxation is legitimate consent.
- Permanent constitutional change; even its author says it's bad policy; it's a hostage bargain artifact.
- The No side's supporters include public safety, educators, nurses, LWV.

My decision. I've weighed both. Key judgment calls:

1. Is the asymmetry a "loophole" that must be closed by raising the citizen-initiative threshold to 2/3, or should majority rule be preserved for local voter self-taxation?

I keep coming back to: the people voting to tax themselves, by majority, is the essence of local democratic self-governance. The "loophole" framing presupposes that the 2/3 rule was intended to bind the people's own initiative power — but the courts held otherwise because the constitution's text says "no local government may impose." Moreover, the initiative route has a built-in check (signature qualification + election). The harms cited (low-turnout elections, "special interests") are speculative relative to the demonstrated, concrete harms of the 2/3 threshold (blocked funding for homelessness response, wildfire protection, etc.).

2. Practical consequences: The LAO itself frames the fiscal impact as "local government tax revenues will not go up as much." Given the state of local finances (federal cuts, deferred infrastructure, wildfire risk, homelessness crisis), making the citizen-initiative special tax route require 2/3 will predictably kill many future funding measures in the 55-66% range. The two-thirds rule for gov-proposed special taxes already exists as a (very high) bar; extending it to citizen initiatives forecloses the main remaining responsive tool.

3. Democratic principle: supermajority requirements for ordinary decisions entrench minority rule. California has plenty of taxpayer protections already (Prop 13 property limits, 2/3 for gov special taxes, 2/3 legislative vote for state tax increases, Gann limit). This measure adds a minority veto over community decisions.

4. The strategic "truce" argument for Yes is real but weak for a single voter: the worse retroactive initiative was already withdrawn and can't return in 2026; if it returns in 2028, voters can fight it then (and the Supreme Court has shown willingness to strike the most sweeping version as an invalid revision). Locking in a permanent constitutional minority veto now to buy temporary peace is a bad trade if the underlying policy is bad.

5. Editorial and civic-group weight: mixed on editorial boards (Bee/BANG/SCNG yes; Press Democrat/Santa Cruz no), but good-government/civic organizations (LWV, SPUR) and the author herself say No. Polls show the electorate leaning No (PPIC 55% no).

Therefore, I conclude "No" is the better vote on Prop 43.

I've seen the Yes arguments in full (ballot arguments + HJTA commentary + Bee/BANG editorials summarized). The Yes case boils down to: uniformity/loophole-closing, taxpayer protection, affordability. I've considered those. The No case: majority rule, local flexibility, service funding, no tax cut, permanent constitutional entrenchment, author opposes.

I'm comfortable with "No."

Actually, let me reflect once more on the strongest Yes argument to make sure I'm not underweighting it: "The system currently lets local officials collude with interest groups to impose taxes with 50%+1 at low-turnout special elections, dodging both the 2/3 threshold and the general-election timing requirement. This is a genuine circumvention of Prop 218's voter protections, and courts can't fix it; only a constitutional amendment can."

Response: (1) Signature-gathering is a significant hurdle that itself requires broad grassroots support; (2) the majority-vote requirement at the election is still a democratic check by the very taxpayers; (3) the problem could be addressed with narrower fixes (e.g., initiatives at general elections only); (4) empirically, the measures passed this way fund widely-shared services and were approved by majorities of 53-62% in high-turnout general elections mostly; (5) the cost of the fix (2/3 for everything) far exceeds the harm. Also the "6% transfer tax" and "2,000 new taxes" claims in the Yes argument are overstated/misleading (SF's 6% top-tier transfer tax predates and isn't a "loophole" creation; the 2,000 figure includes majority-vote general taxes and legally-passed 2/3 special taxes).

Also note: the Yes ballot argument claims Prop 43 "requires governments to spend tax revenue for the specific purpose voters approved" — this is not in the measure's text (it's already implicitly the definition of special tax under Prop 218). That's a misleading claim, which weakens my trust in the Yes case.

Final answer: no.

Let me research this more deeply. Proposition 43 is a California constitutional amendment (ACA 22, Wicks) on the November 3, 2026 ballot. It would raise the vote threshold for voter-initiated local special taxes from a simple majority to two-thirds.

Background:
- Proposition 13 (1978) required two-thirds vote for special taxes.
- Proposition 218 (1996) required two-thirds for special taxes proposed by local governments.
- Court decisions (California Cannabis Coalition v. City of Upland, 2017; and subsequent decisions) allowed special taxes proposed by voters through the initiative process to be approved by a simple majority.
- Prop 43 would close this "loophole" by requiring two-thirds for voter-proposed special taxes too.

Context: It's a deal between state lawmakers and the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association to keep a more restrictive tax proposal (a HJTA initiative) off the ballot. Wait, actually, let me check — the KPBS article says "The measure reflects a deal between state lawmakers and the anti-tax Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association to keep a more restrictive tax proposal off the ballot." Interesting — but actually, I recall that HJTA has an initiative called the "Taxpayer Protection and Government Accountability Act" which was removed from the 2024 ballot by the California Supreme Court. Then they proposed another one for 2026. The deal was that HJTA would withdraw its initiative if lawmakers placed ACA 22 on the ballot.

Wait, but the Berkeley document says "ACA 22, the legislation to place Proposition 43 on the November ballot, is the product of an agreement between state leaders and the Howard..." — presumably Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association.

Also note the FPPC data shows big money on both sides: Support $15.3M (California Business Roundtable Issues PAC with top donors Peter Thiel and Eric Schmidt — interesting), Oppose $7.9M (labor organizations).

2. Arguments and rebuttals

4. The court decisions background (California Cannabis Coalition v. City of Upland)

Let me fetch the LAO analysis and the arguments/rebuttals, plus some news articles.

I need to weigh the arguments:

Pro (Yes on 43):
- Restores Prop 13's two-thirds requirement, closes "loophole" created by courts
- Protects taxpayers from special interests pushing tax increases in low-turnout elections
- Makes initiative taxes subject to the same threshold as government-proposed taxes — consistency
- Prevents ad valorem taxes on real property via initiative
- Some argue the citizen-initiative path allows local governments to collude with allies to circumvent the two-thirds requirement

Con (No on 43):
- Makes it harder for local communities to fund essential services (fire, 911, schools, roads, hospitals, affordable housing)
- Allows 33.4% of voters to veto what ~67% want — anti-majoritarian
- Doesn't cut taxes; it just makes it harder to raise revenue
- Local voters should be able to decide for themselves
- The two-thirds threshold has made it historically very hard to pass taxes; special taxes proposed by governments rarely pass at that threshold

Let me think about the policy merits:

Arguments in favor of Yes (two-thirds threshold):
- Uniformity: government-proposed special taxes need two-thirds; citizen-proposed ones should too, otherwise there's an easy workaround (local officials can recruit allies to run an initiative).
- Tax increases impose costs on everyone, including minorities of voters; supermajority requirements protect against this.
- Closing the loophole prevents strategic use of low-turnout elections.

Arguments in favor of No (keep majority):
- Supermajority requirements are anti-democratic: a minority can block the will of the majority. In practice, taxes that get majority support but not two-thirds fail, meaning communities can't fund services they want.
- Local self-governance: the people of a locality voting to tax themselves for services they want is the essence of local democracy. It's not "special interests" — it requires a majority of local voters.
- California already has trouble funding local services; Prop 13 and 218 have constrained local revenue. This would further constrain.
- The measure is a deal between HJTA and lawmakers to remove a more radical initiative — voting no doesn't bring back the radical initiative (which was withdrawn).
- Historical evidence: special taxes under two-thirds rarely pass; many local measures get 55-66% and would fail under two-thirds.

Hmm, but wait — there's a nuance: Prop 43 would also prohibit local governments (including via initiative) from imposing ad valorem taxes on real property except as permitted under existing constitutional provisions. That's a side provision.

Also, there's a question about whether this would affect school bonds (55% threshold under Prop 39)? No — those are bonds, not taxes, and are governed by other provisions.

Let me think about the "who supports/who opposes" framing:
- Support: Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, California Taxpayers Association, Family Business Association, California Hispanic Chambers of Commerce, California Business Roundtable (with big money from Thiel and Schmidt — interesting, though those donors are noted as top donors to the California Business Roundtable Issues PAC).
- Oppose: California Professional Firefighters, California Federation of Teachers, Nurse Alliance of SEIU CA, League of California Cities? Probably. Labor organizations.

Editorial positions: Let me check what newspapers say. The Mercury News published an op-ed by Hoene (former Legislative Analyst? Actually Mac Taylor? No — Michael Hoene? Chris Hoene was the executive director of the California Budget & Policy Center) against Prop 43. Let me search for editorials.

Let me also check the LA Times coverage, CalMatters coverage, and editorial positions.

I'll also fetch the LAO full analysis and the arguments/rebuttals page.

My own judgment: As an analyst, I should weigh both sides. The question asks for a recommendation. Let me consider what a reasonable, well-researched conclusion would be.

Key considerations:

1. Democratic legitimacy: A supermajority requirement for citizen-initiated taxes means a minority (just over one-third) can block a tax that the majority wants. Taxes fund collective services; if a majority of local voters voluntarily decide to tax themselves for services, blocking that via supermajority is arguably anti-democratic.

2. However, there's the "loophole" concern: courts created a discrepancy. Government-proposed special taxes need 2/3; citizen-proposed need only majority. This creates an incentive for governments to use the initiative process to circumvent the higher threshold — indeed, the LA Times notes "the special interests pushing a tax hike are in some cases aligned with politicians on the measure, blurring the line between who is behind a proposed tax increase." So there's a genuine problem of circumvention.

3. Practical effect: Making all special taxes need 2/3 would make it much harder for local communities to raise revenue for specific services. Research (e.g., from past election data) shows many special taxes pass with 50-66% that would fail at 2/3.

4. The counterargument: if the community really wants it, they can pass a general tax with majority... wait, no — general taxes proposed by governments need majority, but citizen-initiated general taxes? Hmm. Actually, under Prop 218, general taxes proposed by the governing body require a majority vote (and must be at a general election); citizen-initiated general taxes... I believe courts have allowed them with majority too. But a general tax doesn't earmark for specific services; it just goes to the general fund. So communities wanting to fund a specific service like wildfire protection or children's health would have to either use a general tax (less accountability, no earmark) or get 2/3.

Let me look at how other organizations have weighed in: CalMatters, League of Women Voters, editorial boards (LA Times, SF Chronicle, Sac Bee, Mercury News, San Diego Union-Tribune, etc.), California Chamber of Commerce, civil rights groups, etc.

Let me do the research.

Also, I should consider the "deal" context: This was part of a negotiation where HJTA withdrew a more sweeping initiative (the "Taxpayer Protection and Government Accountability Act"). If Prop 43 fails, HJTA might come back with a more sweeping initiative in 2028, which might be worse from a No-voter's perspective. But voting on the merits, that's speculative.

Proposition 43
Limits Voters’ Ability to Raise Revenues for Local Government Services. Legislative Constitutional Amendment.
Analysis of Measure
Background
Local Governments in California. California has many local governments. These include cities, counties, special districts, and school districts.
Vote Thresholds for Local Taxes. The State Constitution allows local governments to increase taxes with local voter approval. Tax increases can be put on a ballot by voters or a local governing board (such as a city council or board of supervisors). Increases in some types of local taxes require a two-thirds vote to approve them, while other types of taxes require a majority (more than half) vote to approve them. Some local tax increases are approved permanently, while others are approved for a limited period of time. Before those taxes expire, voters can be asked whether to extend them.
Proposal
Requires Certain Local Taxes Receive Two-Thirds Approval by Voters. Under current law, local taxes that are used for a specific purpose require a two-thirds vote to be approved. These are called special taxes. However, recent court decisions have allowed special taxes that are proposed by voters to be approved with a majority vote. Under Proposition 43, beginning on January 1, 2027, any new, increased, or extended local special taxes proposed by voters would require a two-thirds vote.
Fiscal Effects
Possibility for Lower Local Government Tax Revenues in the Future. Proposition 43 makes it harder for local governments to pass certain taxes. As a result, local governments' tax revenues could be lower in the future than they otherwise would be. The actual revenue impact is unknown and would depend on future decisions by local governments and voters.
Yes/No Statement
A YES vote on this measure means: Certain local government taxes would require two-thirds approval by voters.
A NO vote on this measure means: Certain local government taxes could continue to be approved by voters with a majority vote.
Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact
Possibility that local government tax revenues will not go up as much in the future due to a higher vote threshold for certain taxes.
Ballot Label
Fiscal Impact : Possibility that local government tax revenues will not go up as much in the future due to a higher vote threshold for certain taxes.

PROP
43
LIMITS VOTERS’ ABILITY TO RAISE REVENUES FOR LOCAL GOVERNMENT SERVICES. LEGISLATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 43
VOTE YES ON PROP. 43: THE LOCAL TAXPAYER PROTECTION ACT
California families are struggling with the highest income, sales, and gas taxes in the nation. Yet politicians and special interests keep pushing higher taxes that make our cost of living even more expensive.
We can’t afford to pay ANY MORE in new or higher taxes. PROP. 43 RESTORES PROPOSITION 13 TAXPAYER PROTECTIONS
Proposition 13 was designed to make it harder to raise taxes, but court decisions created loopholes that allow special interests to impose massive new tax increases by circumventing the taxpayer protections voters approved. Californians are paying billions in new or higher taxes they would not have to pay if it weren’t for these loopholes. Prop. 43 closes these loopholes and restores the two-thirds vote requirement to pass local special taxes.
PROP. 43 MAKES IT HARDER TO RAISE YOUR TAXES
Local governments have imposed over 2,000 new or higher taxes in the past decade, including higher sales, property and utility taxes-using the loopholes courts created in Prop. 13 to impose some of the most costly and damaging tax increases Californians face today.
These new and higher taxes make everything we buy or use more expensive, from food and gas to utilities and housing.
Prop. 43 guarantees voters the right to vote on all local taxes and restores the two-thirds vote for special local taxes.
PROP. 43 PROTECTS HOMEOWNERS FROM COSTLY NEW REAL ESTATE TAXES
California already has some of the highest housing costs in America, yet special interests are using court-created loopholes to add new taxes on the sale of homes, apartments and other real estate.
Some cities now charge real estate transfer taxes as high as 6%. For California’s median-priced home of $900,000, that would cost a homeowner $54,000 simply for selling their house. Those costs steal homeowners’ equity, raise apartment rents, and make building new housing more expensive.
Prop. 43 makes it much harder for special interests to impose these costly taxes on homeowners, renters, and small businesses.
PROP. 43 STOPS THE BAIT-AND-SWITCH TAX TRICKS
Politicians and special interests promise new taxes will fund schools, roads, and public safety-only to divert the money elsewhere and frustrate the will of voters. Prop. 43 requires governments to spend tax revenue for the specific purpose voters approved and restores the broad voter support required before politicians and special interests impose earmarked tax measures.
If taxpayers are asked to pay more, they deserve the right to vote and the confidence their money will be spent as promised.
PROP. 43 PUTS VOTERS BACK IN CHARGE
Every election, politicians say they need just one more tax increase. Prop. 43 simply ensures TAXPAYERS are fully protected by the right to vote on taxes.
Vote YES on Prop. 43:
• Affirms the voters’ right to vote on all new or higher local taxes. • Restores the two-thirds vote requirement for local special taxes. • Protects Proposition 13 and closes court-created loopholes. • Makes it harder for special interests to raise taxes. • Protects homeowners, renters, and small businesses from new real estate taxes. • Strengthens accountability for how taxpayer dollars are spent.

REBUTTAL TO ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 43
We all want relief from California’s high cost of living. But Proposition 43 doesn’t cut your taxes a penny. It attacks something far more valuable: the power of your vote.
PROP. 43 WEAKENS YOUR VOTE.
Today, when local voters decide how to fund their communities, the majority rules. Prop. 43 throws that out, letting just 33.4% of voters veto what nearly 67% want. Under Prop. 43, a NO vote counts twice as much as a YES. That isn’t fair, and it isn’t democracy.
PROP. 43 DEEPENS THE HOUSING CRISIS.
Across California, communities vote to build affordable homes for working families, seniors, and veterans. They are helping renters stay housed and move people off the streets. Prop. 43 hands a small minority the power to block those solutions, even when a clear majority of your neighbors support them.
PROP. 43 TIES YOUR COMMUNITY’S HANDS.
Prop. 43 makes it harder for you to fund the critical local services your community counts on: staffing fire stations and 911 response, preparing neighborhoods for wildfire, repairing crumbling roads, keeping schools, parks, and libraries open, and protecting local hospitals and clinics as Washington cuts healthcare funding. When funding is blocked, help arrives slower, classrooms grow more crowded, and communities are left less safe.
KEEP THE POWER WHERE IT BELONGS-WITH YOU AND YOUR NEIGHBORS.
That’s why teachers, nurses, firefighters, and housing advocates all oppose Prop. 43.
VOTE NO ON PROPOSITION 43.

ARGUMENT AGAINST PROPOSITION 43
PROPOSITION 43 LIMITS VOTERS’ ABILITY TO FUND ESSENTIAL LOCAL SERVICES.
Prop. 43 makes it harder for you to fund critical services like police and fire departments, fix and repair local roads, staff our local schools or backfill federal healthcare cuts. Prop. 43 undermines the voice of voters and the majority vote by letting just one-third of voters (33.4%) block local voter decisions-and it makes it easier for corporate special interests to avoid paying their fair share.
PROP. 43 MAKES IT HARDER TO FUND FIRE AND POLICE SERVICES.
Local police and firefighters can’t rely on Sacramento or Washington politicians. These services are funded at the local level. Prop. 43 wants to make it harder for local voters to direct new funding to services like police and fire. Without adequate funding, 911 response times are slower, fire stations sit understaffed, and families wait longer for help when every second counts. When a house fire breaks out-or a wildfire threatens our neighborhoods-that local funding is what protects us. Prop. 43 would let a small minority of voters block it. Even if 66% of voters say yes, Prop. 43 would prevent us from funding desperately needed local services.
PROP. 43 MAKES IT HARDER TO FIX ROADS, FUND SCHOOLS, AND PROTECT HEALTHCARE.
Across California, local voters have come together to repair crumbling roads and improve transportation, to fund their neighborhood schools, and to protect local hospitals and healthcare-especially as Washington cuts federal health funding. These are decisions communities make for themselves, by majority vote. Instead, Prop. 43 hands a small group of voters the power to veto those solutions, even when the majority supports them.
PROP. 43 EMPOWERS 33.4% OF VOTERS OVER THE WILL OF THE MAJORITY.
In America, we believe in one person, one vote-and the majority wins. Prop. 43 throws that out. It empowers just over one-third of voters to block what nearly 67% want. It puts the out-voted minority in charge-even if they are extremists. It makes their NO vote count twice as much as a YES vote.
CORPORATE DONORS BENEFIT. NOT TAXPAYERS.
Under Prop. 43, corporate donors who spend big in elections will benefit most. Right now, voters can hold these corporations and developers accountable at the ballot box, and make them pay their fair share for local needs. Prop. 43 is designed to take that power away-to protect the powerful few, at everyone else’s expense.

Vote NO to protect your vote and majority rule. Keep the power where it belongs-with you and your neighbors.
VOTE NO ON PROPOSITION 43.

REBUTTAL TO ARGUMENT AGAINST
PROPOSITION 43
VOTE YES ON PROP. 43 TO RESTORE TAXPAYER PROTECTIONS
Californians already pay high taxes. But instead of prioritizing funding for critical services like police and fire, local politicians waste your money on their pet projects- then demand tax increases, claiming the need to fund the most important priorities.
The state Constitution requires a two-thirds vote for taxes earmarked for a specific purpose, but recent court decisions created a loophole that allowed special taxes to pass with fewer votes. Now Californians are paying billions in taxes they should not have had to pay.
Prop. 43 RESTORES the longstanding two-thirds vote requirement for local special taxes, protecting homeowners, renters, and small businesses from costly new sales and parcel taxes, taxes on electricity and gas, and real estate taxes.
Prop. 43 GUARANTEES taxpayers the right to vote on new or higher local taxes and requires governments to spend taxpayer dollars for the specific purposes voters approved-preventing bait-and-switch schemes that make our sky-high cost of living even worse.
Over the last decade, local governments have imposed 2,000 new or higher taxes. Prop. 43 CLOSES LOOPHOLES used to pass some of the most damaging tax increases, restores the protections voters originally approved under Proposition 13, and makes it harder for special interests to raise taxes without broad voter support.
The Legislature’s nearly unanimous vote to place Prop. 43 on the ballot sends a clear message: activist courts exceeded voters’ intent by creating loopholes that weakened Proposition 13’s protections.
Restore your right to vote on ALL local taxes.
VOTE YES ON PROP. 43

# California Cannabis Coalition v. UplandAnnotate this Case
The Supreme Court of California held that, in light of the text and other indicia of the purpose associated with the relevant constitutional and statutory provisions, Cal.
Const., art.
XIII C, section 2 does not limit voters' power to raise taxes by statutory initiative.
The court explained that a contrary conclusion would require an unreasonably broad construction of the term "local government" at the expense of the people’s constitutional right to direct democracy, undermining the longstanding and consistent view that courts should protect and liberally construe it.
In this case, the California Cannabis Coalition drafted a medical marijuana initiative proposing to repeal an existing City ordinance.
The Coalition subsequently petitioned for a writ of mandate when the City failed to submit the initiative to the voters at a special election.
The supreme court affirmed the court of appeal's holding that article XIII C, section 2 only governs levies that are imposed by local government, and thus directed the superior court to issue a writ of mandate compelling the City to place the initiative on a special ballot in accordance with Elections Code section 9214.

I believe Measure A 2024 was placed on the ballot via initiative by homeless advocates (united way etc.) precisely to use the majority-vote route. It passed with about 53-54%. Under Prop 43, it would have failed. Also Berkeley Measure P (2018, soda tax), Oakland soda taxes (2016), SF Prop C (2018, 61%), Prop W... Albany, Richmond... These soda taxes were citizen initiatives passing ~50-70%. Berkeley Measure O (2020)? Culver City? Also SF's Prop C (2018, homeless services tax on corporations, 61%) — passed via initiative after Board of Supervisors couldn't put it at 2/3? Actually SF Prop C (2018) was placed by signature... it was backed by Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff, qualified via signatures, passed 60.9%. SF later passed Prop M (2024) restructuring...

Also there were 2020-2024 examples: Monterey County Measure...? Humboldt? Mendocino? Various school parcel taxes (those are gov-proposed, 2/3). The citizen-initiative route has been used in: SF (Prop C 2018, Prop W 2018 free city college), Oakland (2020 Measure Q parks... passed 53%?; Measure S homeless?; Measure T?; Measure U oakland affordable housing 2021, 67.7%? passed just above 2/3), LA (Measure ULA 2022, 57.8%), LA County (Measure A 2024, ~53%), Culver City 2024...? El Monte, Santa Cruz (Measure C 2025?), Santa Clara County (Measure A 2025), Sonoma (Measure H 2024, 62%)... wait, Sonoma Measure H was described by CalMatters: "In 2024, 62% of Sonoma County voters backed a half-cent sales tax to fund wildfire response and other emergency services." Was it citizen-initiated? Probably yes (or extended existing?). Anyway.

So the practical effect: a bunch of major revenue measures — LA County Measure A (homelessness, ~$1B/yr), LA City ULA (~$300-900M/yr intended), SF Prop C 2018 (~$300M/yr), etc. — passed with 53-62% and would have failed under 2/3. Under Prop 43, all future such measures would need 2/3.

The Yes side says: that's the point — these taxes were enacted without the constitutionally required broad support; courts eroded Prop 13/218.

Now, the fundamental policy question: Should special taxes (earmarked) require 2/3 regardless of who proposes them, or majority?

Arguments for 2/3 (Yes):
- Earmarked taxes bind future spending and impose on everyone; broad consensus justified.
- Consistency and anti-circumvention: Otherwise local officials can collude with allies to run "citizen" initiatives at low-turnout special elections, dodging both the 2/3 requirement AND the general-election timing requirement. (Upland also held initiatives can go on special election ballots.) This is a real governance concern: strategic timing + majority threshold = easy tax passage without broad consent. Though the initiative process itself requires signature gathering.
- Restores what voters intended in 1978/1996.
- Protects taxpayers/affordability in a high-cost, high-tax state.

Arguments for majority (No):
- One person, one vote; a tax approved by 60% of the people is democratically legitimate. Requiring 2/3 lets 1/3 impose its will — the opposite of majority rule — and empirically entrenches the status quo (which post-Prop 13 underfunds local services).
- Local self-determination: communities know their needs (wildfire protection in Sonoma, homelessness in LA).
- The signature requirement + majority election is itself a high bar; there's no evidence of rampant abuse.
- Fiscal needs: LAO notes revenues will be lower; with federal Medicaid cuts and state deficits, local safety nets need funding.
- Real-world examples of measures that would have failed: fire protection, homelessness services, healthcare.
- Even the author urges No; the measure is a hostage-exchange artifact, not considered policy. And the ballot title itself: "Limits Voters' Ability to Raise Revenues for Local Government Services."
- Money behind it: CA Business Roundtable (Thiel, Schmidt as top donors) — $10.69M; real estate/anti-ULA interests. Hmm wait, actually Thiel and Schmidt being top donors of the CA Business Roundtable Issues PAC is interesting but that PAC supports multiple things. Let me not overweight that.

Also consider the counterargument that the No side is heavily union-funded ($7.9M) — public employee unions benefit from local tax revenue. So both sides have interested money.

Neutral-ish observers: 
- SPUR: No.
- Press Democrat: No ("Prop. 43 wants to fix a system that isn't broken"; "The system, admittedly, is strange, but it works.")
- Santa Cruz Sentinel: No with reservations.
- Sac Bee: Yes ("Close ballot-box taxing loophole").
- Mercury News/East Bay Times (BANG): Yes ("Back Prop. 43 to restore voter-approved restrictions on local taxes").
- Southern California News Group (Daily Bulletin etc.): Yes.
- League of Women Voters? Let me check. California League of Cities? CSAC (counties) — presumably No. Let me check LWV and other good-government groups.

Also, I should think about the "which is better" question from the perspective of overall welfare and governance:

My assessment of the strongest points:

1. On pure democratic principle: majority rule should be the default for local self-taxation. The people voting to tax themselves — via initiative — is direct democracy at its most legitimate. A 2/3 requirement means a 66.6% supermajority is needed, i.e., 33.4% can veto. For a state constitutional amendment to permanently disable this local democratic tool statewide seems like overkill for addressing the "loophole" problem.

2. The loophole/circumvention concern is real but can be addressed more narrowly (e.g., requiring initiatives to appear at general elections, or requiring that government-backed "citizen" initiatives meet the 2/3 bar). Instead, Prop 43 applies 2/3 to ALL citizen-initiated special taxes, including genuine grassroots ones (e.g., Sonoma fire protection). The measure is a blunt instrument.

3. Empirical effect: It will block many majority-supported local revenue measures for essential services. In a state with chronic local fiscal stress (post-Prop 13), and with federal cuts, this will predictably worsen service funding. The LAO's fiscal note confirms the direction (lower revenues).

4. Taxpayer protection argument: California taxes are high in some respects, and the cost of living is brutal. But the answer to high taxes should be prioritization/spending reform, not structurally disabling local majorities from funding fire departments. Also note that general taxes (majority-vote, but must be at general elections and are unearmarked) remain available to local governments placed by councils; the citizen special tax initiative was one of the few ways communities could earmark for specific priorities. Under Prop 43, the option remains but at 2/3 — historically very hard (though not impossible; e.g., many 2/3 measures do pass, particularly parcel taxes in affluent areas).

Hmm, wait — but I should also consider: is there something to the idea that the 2/3 threshold "ensures broad consensus" and that many special taxes do pass at 2/3? Yes — in wealthy, liberal areas, parcel taxes routinely get 67-75%. But statewide, the pass rate at 2/3 is much lower. E.g., data from California City Finance/Edwin Park: special tax measures (2/3) pass around 50-60% of the time, vs general taxes (majority) ~80%+.

5. The "it's a deal/truce" argument for Yes: If Prop 43 fails, HJTA revives its initiative for 2028, which could be worse (retroactive repeals, broader 2/3 on fees, etc.). But: (a) the CA Supreme Court in Padilla (2024) already showed willingness to strike the broader version as an unconstitutional revision; (b) a future initiative would need to pass a statewide vote — uncertain; (c) accepting permanent policy you think is bad to avoid a hypothetical worse policy is a questionable trade; (d) in fact, Wicks and others calculate that voting No and fighting later is better. Also, the truce already achieved its main purpose (removing the 2026 HJTA initiative); a No vote doesn't restore it.

Hmm, but actually, let me reconsider: is the concern that HJTA's withdrawn initiative "would have devastated revenues for local governments and retroactively rescinded some local tax increases" — and if Prop 43 fails, HJTA will qualify it for 2028 and might win? Prop 43's own polling shows it trailing (No leading by ~10). A 2028 HJTA initiative would face similar headwinds but with different framing ("Taxpayer Protection Act") might pass. Uncertain.

6. There's also a fairness/consistency argument the other way: Why should a city council's special tax need 2/3 but a citizens' identical special tax need only majority? Two responses: (i) The initiative power is a constitutional right held by the people, and constraining it requires clear language (the Upland reasoning — courts won't construe statutes/constitutional provisions to limit the initiative power absent clarity); (ii) the asymmetry could also be fixed by lowering the government-proposed threshold... but that would require voter approval too and nobody proposed it. Given only one option is on the ballot, the question is whether the asymmetry as it stands is so harmful that it must be closed in the restrictive direction.

Actually, here's a subtle point: the practical "circumvention" is that city councils and mayors support "citizen" initiatives to get their preferred taxes through at majority. Examples: LA ULA had active support from councilmembers? Actually ULA was pushed by unions/housing groups; the city attorney put it on the ballot after signatures were verified. SF Prop C 2018 — Benioff-backed, opposed by the mayor and Board of Supervisors initially? Actually supervisors eventually supported? Not sure. LA County Measure A 2024 — was pushed by initiative (United Way, service providers) after Measure H (2/3, 69.5% in 2017) was set to expire; the county supported it. So yes, there's a pattern: when advocates know they can't hit 2/3 with a council-placed measure, they gather signatures for a majority-vote initiative. That IS a workaround of Prop 218's intent.

But is that workaround bad for the public? The workaround still requires a majority of voters to approve. Prop 218's 2/3 requirement for special taxes was itself a 1996 initiative (Howard Jarvis Association) that constrained local government. The "intent" of Prop 218's drafters was 2/3 for special taxes; but the language they wrote said "no local government may impose... approved by a two-thirds vote." The court read that literally. One can argue the drafters' sloppy language shouldn't be rescued at the expense of the initiative power.

From a voter's perspective in 2026: Do I want my community to be able to enact earmarked local taxes by majority vote via initiative? If yes → vote No on 43. Do I want broad consensus (2/3) for any tax? → vote Yes.

My own judgment: I find the No position more persuasive, primarily because:

(a) The anti-majoritarian structure of supermajority requirements is a strong democratic objection, especially for taxes that a community imposes on itself by direct vote. The "protection" being offered is protection from one's own majority — the people are the taxpayers.

(b) The practical consequences — blocking funding for fire, emergency response, homelessness, healthcare, housing that 55-66% of local voters support — are significant and negative for public welfare, particularly in an era of federal retrenchment. LA County Measure A (homelessness sales tax, ~$1.1B/yr) passed with ~53%... wait, hmm, would Measure A have passed at 2/3? No. So without the initiative route, LA County would have lost Measure H replacement funding. That's a big deal given the homelessness crisis.

Hold on — one consideration: maybe voters in a community SHOULD need 2/3 to impose earmarked taxes because earmarking constrains fiscal flexibility and because taxes fall on everyone (including the 47% minority). But the general tax (majority-vote) route already exists for councils; earmarking is a feature (accountability), not a bug. Requiring 2/3 for accountability-enhancing earmarks while allowing majority for general taxes creates weird incentives (governments just do general taxes and promise to spend on X — less enforceable).

(c) The measure is a permanent constitutional change crafted as a political bargain, opposed by its own author, and its ballot-case in favor rests on some questionable claims (e.g., the "bait-and-switch"/spending guarantee claim isn't actually in the text; the "2,000 new taxes" figure conflates general and special taxes; the "6% transfer tax" claim is about Oakland's... actually Oakland's transfer tax is 1.5%? Actually, "Some cities now charge real estate transfer taxes as high as 6%" — hmm, that might refer to SF's commercial transfer tax tiers? No... Let me think: Santa Fe? Hmm. Berkeley Measure P (2018)? No. Anyway.)

(d) Editorial split: some credible papers say Yes (Sac Bee, BANG), some say No (Press Democrat, Santa Cruz Sentinel). The polling shows the public leaning No.

Also California Teachers Association, firefighters, nurses — No. Chambers of commerce (Cal Chamber?) — Yes presumably. Let me check CalChamber's position — they usually do "job killer" lists. Schaben, Los Angeles Times via Getty Images In summary The measure would require two-thirds of voters to approve any local special taxes, instead of the simple majority for citizen-led initiatives. Anti-tax advocates say it should be that hard for governments to tax Californians, but local officials say it could constrain funding for essential services. Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called. In 2022, 58% of Los Angeles city voters approved a hefty tax on mansion sales. In 2024, 62% of Sonoma County voters backed a half-cent sales tax to fund wildfire response and other emergency services. Neither would have become law under the threshold set by Proposition 43 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-43-tax-threshold/), which would require a two-thirds vote to pass any local tax measures that pay for specific services. Anti-tax advocates such as the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, which helped get Prop. 43 on the ballot, say it should be harder (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/08/california-constitution-proposition-43-taxes/) to tax Californians in a state where tax rates are already high. They argue that the measure would apply an equal standard to whoever wants a special tax, whether the government or citizen groups. Californians voted in 1996 (https://lao.ca.gov/1996/120196_prop_218/understanding_prop218_1296.html) to establish a two-thirds threshold for special tax measures. For decades, it was widely assumed that the threshold applied to all special taxes — until 2017, when the state Supreme Court said (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2017/08/state-supreme-court-made-easier-raise-taxes/) the law specifically applied only to tax measures put on the ballot by local officials. But what about special taxes proposed by citizens? The court declined to clarify (https://calmatters.org/economy/2019/02/local-tax-chaos-california-supreme-court/). Confusion ensued. Since then, several high-profile local special tax measures placed on the ballot by nongovernmental groups have passed with a simple majority. Local government officials, labor unions and affordable housing advocates oppose the measure, arguing the proposal would make it difficult to collect revenues for essential services, such as firefighting, education and healthcare. They argue it would allow “minority rule (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/08/proposition-43-taxes-minority-rule/)” because it would only take a third of voters to block special taxes. Jon Coupal, president of the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, said Prop. 43 would clarify that the two-thirds rule applies to all special taxes. He said that the two-thirds vote requirement dates to the 1849 state Constitution, which required a supermajority vote of state lawmakers to ask voters to borrow money. “The power to tax is (the) government’s most draconian power,” he told CalMatters. “The people of the state of California have made it a policy that when you are going to exercise that power, it should require a higher degree of consensus.” But opponents say the initiative risks kneecapping funding for local services. Darrell Roberts, president of the California Professional Firefighters union, which represents 38,000 firefighters, called Prop. 43 an insurmountable roadblock (https://www.marinij.com/2026/10/03/opinion-prop-43-sacrifices-local-public-safety-to-protect-corporate-profits/) to raising money for community services. This November, Los Angeles voters will decide on a half-cent sales tax (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-06/lapd-union-will-oppose-half-cent-sales-tax-hike-pushed-by-firefighters-union) proposal to hire more firefighters, Roberts noted. “Under Prop. 43, it’s clear that the powerful few would be protected at the expense of everyone else,” he wrote in the Marin Independent Journal. Supporters have poured almost $15 million into the measure, nearly $10 million of it from the California Business Roundtable PAC. Opponents have collected $6 million, with the biggest contribution, $1.5 million, from a PAC affiliated with the Service Employees International Union of California. Sign up for free Δ Prop. 43 originated from L.A.’s ‘mansion tax’ fight Prop. 43 stems from a bitter fight over Los Angeles’ “mansion tax,” a 4% tax on real estate sales of more than $5.3 million and 5.5% on sales more than $10.6 million. The tax rates rise with inflation. It has generated $1.4 billion (https://housing.lacity.gov/ula-revenue) in revenue since it became law in 2023, according to the city. The tax angered real estate developers (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/04/proposition-realty-mansion-tax-jarvis/) and business groups, who said it impeded new construction of all kinds of developments, including affordable housing. The opposition fueled a campaign led by Coupal’s group earlier this year to qualify a ballot measure that would have slashed real estate sales taxes statewide, applied the two-thirds vote requirement to all special taxes and revoked taxes that previously passed by a simple majority, such as the mansion tax. Prop. 43 is a more modest proposal resulting from an eleventh-hour negotiation between Coupal and Democratic leaders in the state Legislature to kill the more extensive version. Assemblymember Buffy Wicks (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/buffy-wicks-165044), an Oakland Democrat, authored the compromise language (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260aca22). The measure is limited to the vote threshold and does not apply retroactively to taxes such as the mansion tax. Just days after the Legislature placed Prop. 43 on the ballot, Wicks said she is “adamantly opposed” to it. “The clock was running out, and we had a choice to make: Leave a retroactive measure on the ballot that threatened billions in local funding, or accept a much narrower constitutional amendment that I still believed was bad policy,” Wicks said (https://bsky.app/profile/buffywicks.bsky.social/post/3mpi3t4tkmp2h) in a social media post. Is there public appetite? This isn’t Coupal’s first rodeo. In 2024, his group sponsored a much broader ballot measure to make it harder to raise taxes, but the California Supreme Court unanimously blocked (https://calmatters.org/politics/2024/06/california-taxes-supreme-court-ballot/) it before the election, deeming it an illegal attempt to change the state’s constitution. How will a narrower Prop. 43 perform this year? A September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) from the nonpartisan Public Policy Institute of California found 51% of likely voters would vote no on Prop. 43, versus just 43% who would vote yes. But Coupal hopes the proposal taps into voters’ concerns about affordability and their frustration with the high cost of living in California. “We are in a general climate right now where Californians really feel overtaxed,” he said. “California needs to prioritize its spending before it asks for more.” READ NEXT Why are out-of-state billionaires funding a California voter ID measure? Prop. 43 would make special taxes harder to pass. That’s the point, say anti-tax advocates

By Yue Stella Yu, CalMatters

This story was originally published by CalMatters. Sign up for their newsletters.

In 2022, 58% of Los Angeles city voters approved a hefty tax on mansion sales.

In 2024, 62% of Sonoma County voters backed a half-cent sales tax to fund wildfire response and other emergency services.

Neither would have become law under the threshold set by Proposition 43, which would require a two-thirds vote to pass any local tax measures that pay for specific services. 

Anti-tax advocates such as the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, which helped get Prop. 43 on the ballot, say it should be harder to tax Californians in a state where tax rates are already high. They argue that the measure would apply an equal standard to whoever wants a special tax, whether the government or citizen groups.

Californians voted in 1996 to establish a two-thirds threshold for special tax measures. For decades, it was widely assumed that the threshold applied to all special taxes — until 2017, when the state Supreme Court said the law specifically applied only to tax measures put on the ballot by local officials. 

But what about special taxes proposed by citizens? The court declined to clarify. Confusion ensued. Since then, several high-profile local special tax measures placed on the ballot by nongovernmental groups have passed with a simple majority.

Local government officials, labor unions and affordable housing advocates oppose the measure, arguing the proposal would make it difficult to collect revenues for essential services, such as firefighting, education and healthcare.
